item.title: Selective Pd-Catalyzed C(sp3)−H Functionalization of Carbocyclic β-Amino Acids: Toward the Late-Stage C−H Functionalization of α,β-Hybrid Peptides
item.description: Carbocyclic β-amino acids are highly attractive scaffolds in medicinal chemistry, in foldamer sciences as well as in organic chemistry, where they are used as catalysts. However, unlike their widely available unsubstituted counterparts, general strategies for the synthesis of carbo-functionalized derivatives remain scarce. Herein, we report the selective synthesis of C4-substituted all-cis and cis-trans 2-aminocyclobutane-1-carboxylic acids (ACBC) derivatives by Pd-catalyzed C–H carbo-functionalization with excellent regio- and diastereoselectivity using an aminoquinoline auxiliary at C1. This approach tolerates a broad range of coupling partners, including (hetero)aryl, alkenyl, alkynyl, and alkyl groups, and can be extended to 2-aminocyclopentane-1-carboxylic acid (ACPC) and 2-aminocyclohexane-1-carboxylic acid (ACHC) derivatives, providing step-economical access to unprecedented carbocyclic β-amino acids. A one-pot C−H arylation/epimerization sequence further provides access to the corresponding all-trans ACBC. Beyond the synthesis of structurally diverse carbocyclic β-amino acids, the versatility of the method was also demonstrated by the regio- and stereoselective late-stage C(sp3)−H arylation of C-terminal ACBC residues in enantiopure α/β-hybrid peptides, offering a direct route to the diversification of conformationally constrained peptide architectures.

item.title: Homopropargylglycine Lowers the Background Floor in Tandem Mass Tag-Based Protein Degradation Profiling
Bridging the Gap Between Material Discovery and Practical Electrodes: Identifying Scaling Limits in High-Capacity Anodes
item.description: High-capacity conversion and alloying anodes often deliver gravimetric capacities at low mass loading that cannot be retained in practical, high-loading electrodes. Conventional electrochemical metrics do not identify when additional loading stops contributing proportionally to the areal capacity. Here, we use a two-timescale analysis of chronoamperometric measurements to extract characteristic relaxation times and test them as descriptors of electrode scalability. Using SnFe2O4 electrodes from two syntheses and two active-material contents, we show that the slower relaxation time, τ1, describes the loss of scaling efficiency across materials and formulations. Normalising τ1 by electrode thickness or by the active-material volume does not improve this description. SnFe2O4 and Ga2O3 electrodes that reach a maximum in areal capacity do so within a few-fold range of τ1. Thus, the position of an electrode relative to this range identifies electrodes that are promising candidates for higher mass loading. Placing SnFe2O4 electrodes reported in the literature on an areal capacity– τ1 map identifies such candidates from routinely reported rate-capability data.

item.title: Photocontraction of Thietane Dioxides: A Modular Route to Functionalized Cyclopropanes
item.description: Cyclopropanes are important structural motifs in medicinal chemistry, and considerable efforts have been devoted to developing synthetic methods that accommodate diverse substitution patterns and functional-group profiles. Within the synthetic toolbox, ring-contraction strategies remain relatively underexplored, despite their potential to enable late-stage ring construction, provide access to challenging substitution patterns, and reduce reliance on protecting-group manipulations. In this context, we developed a modular approach to access functionalized 2-arylcyclopropanes based on the photochemical SO2 extrusion from thietane dioxides. The method offers synthetic flexibility through complementary and straightforward precursor syntheses involving sulfene-alkene [2+2] cycloaddition or nucleophilic addition to thiete dioxides. The contraction process is catalyst-free, requires neither highly reactive reagents nor stoichiometric metal reagents and accommodates a broad range of N-, O-, P-, and C-based substituents. Its synthetic utility is demonstrated through the development of one-pot nucleophilic addition-photocontraction sequences, integration with skeletal editing to convert oxetanes into cyclopropanes, and implementation in continuous flow using UV LEDs irradiation. Experimental and computational investigations support a mechanism initiated by triplet-state fragmentation, followed by stereospecific cyclization of a singlet diradicaloid with concomitant SO2 extrusion. This work establishes photochemical SO2 extrusion as a versatile ring-contraction strategy complementary to established approaches to functionalized cyclopropanes.

item.title: VeSMA: GPU-native library for retrosynthetic expansion and beyond
item.description: Template­based computer­aided synthesis planning generates candidate precursors by applying retrosynthetic reaction templates to target molecules. Applying these templates across large collections of molecules is computationally demanding, as each application requires both identifying matching molecular patterns and construct­ ing the resulting precursors. Here we present VeSMA, a reaction­template application library with dedicated NVIDIA CUDA, Apple Metal, and CPU backends accessible through a unified interface. To our knowledge, VeSMA is the first implementation to execute the complete reaction­template application pipeline on GPUs, rather than accelerating only template selection or substructure matching. VeSMA enumerates distinct template matches, applies the corresponding graph transformations, constructs precursor molecules, and updates the number of hydrogen atoms and recalculates aromaticity. We evaluate VeSMA using the PaRoutes collection of published multi­ step retrosynthetic routes and reaction templates derived from USPTO patents, testing agreement across backends and with established reaction engines, as well as its use in successive retrosynthetic steps. Across nearly 770 000 confirmed molecule–template pairs, VeSMA and RDChiral produce identical precursor outcome sets for 98.3% of pairs when stereochemistry is excluded from the comparison. We further measure reaction­ application throughput and demonstrate integration into an exhaustive depth­two expansion. VeSMA is released as a library for integration into retrosynthetic planning workflows, benchmarking, and further development.

item.title: Nano-Flow Cytometry for Quality Control of Coated and Antibody-Functionalized DNA Origami
item.description: DNA origami can display targeting ligands with nanometer precision, but their use in vivo is limited by poor stability and by the accessibility of the ligands they present. Protective coatings that address the first problem may worsen the second. Nano-flow cytometry (nFCM), which records side scatter and multicolor fluorescence of nanoparticles in solution at high throughput, is evaluated for quality control of coated and antibody-functionalized DNA origami. Origami are detected label-free as an increase in violet side-scatter events, although most scatter below the acquisition trigger, and a dilution series shows that event rates increase sub-linearly with concentration, so events are not single-particle counts. Within these limits, nFCM identifies residual silica particulates and sample-dependent clustering in coated preparations. A scatter gain consistent with a silica shell appears only at the higher precursor ratio, and a poly-L-lysine–poly(ethylene glycol) (PLL-PEG) coating is not detected by scatter. Two-color coincidence detection reveals biotin-specific antibody binding as a ~1% excess of origami–antibody coincidences over a no-biotin control. This excess is about twofold smaller on PLL-PEG-coated origami (apparent penalty of at most about 0.7 kT). These results establish nFCM as a complementary quality-control tool for DNA nanostructures and identify the acquisition conditions that limit absolute quantification.

item.title: Interfragment Population Suppression in Density Functional Theory
item.description: Excessive electron delocalization in semilocal density functional theory can lead to overbinding in molecular complexes. Interfragment population suppression (IPS) addresses this problem by constraining the electron population in the region where the fragment densities overlap. IPS estimates the target depletion from the electronic structure of the unconstrained complex using one fitted parameter per functional. The density then relaxes self-consistently under the constraint, and the energy is evaluated with the parent functional. For both PBE-D4 and SCAN, IPS improves the dissociation curves of neutral and ionic hydrogen-bonded dimers, with the largest corrections at short range. The integrated electron population on the proton-donor side of the hydrogen bond also moves closer to the relaxed MP2 reference. Applied pairwise, IPS reduces overbinding in all eight water-hexamer isomers, lowering the mean absolute error in total interaction energies from 3.96 to 1.46 kcal/mol for PBE-D4 and from 5.11 to 1.36 kcal/mol for SCAN. In ion–water clusters, this pairwise treatment improves the two-body interaction energies of all four anionic clusters. Together, these results show that a constraint on the interfragment electron population can reduce overbinding in hydrogen-bonded dimers and clusters while retaining the parent exchange–correlation functional.

item.title: Patterning Capture Oligonucleotides on DUV-Defined Silicon Sites: Toward Sequence-Programmable DNA Origami Placement
item.description: Combining top-down lithography with DNA self-assembly could place molecularly defined structures at chosen positions in semiconductor devices. Placement of DNA origami on lithographic patterns currently relies on Mg2+-mediated adsorption, which is sensitive to ionic conditions and cannot distinguish origami by sequence. As a step toward sequence-programmable placement, we pattern capture oligonucleotides on silicon sites defined by deep-ultraviolet (DUV) photolithography. Silanizing through the developed photoresist, and removing the resist before the oligonucleotide is applied, confines the functional layer to the sites. Amine-terminated, Cy5-labelled strands were retained on the sites with three coupling chemistries: epoxide (GPTMS), EDC/NHS-activated carboxyl (CTES) and aldehyde (APTES with glutaraldehyde). In preliminary deposition experiments on GPTMS-functionalized chips, incubation with 1 nM square origami tiles carrying complementary extensions left features 40–60 nm across on the functionalized regions and none detectable on the surrounding oxide by SEM. These features were absent from a chip carrying capture strands only, and by AFM the sites of the tile-incubated chip were 0.8–1.4 nm higher and about three times rougher than those of the capture-strand-only chip. The features were also absent from the sites of a chip incubated with 10 nM tiles, their shape was not resolved, and triangle-based pentagonal and hexagonal assemblies were not found on the sites. Whether attachment depends on the capture sequence has not yet been tested. We set out the controls, surface passivation and imaging needed to establish hybridization-directed placement of single origami on DUV-defined sites.

item.title: Bayesian Optimization for Constructing Quantum Control Fields in Optically-Excited Heterostructure Nanomaterials
item.description: We present a high-dimensional machine learning framework based on Bayesian optimization (BO) for constructing optimal control fields to drive targeted quantum-state transitions in nanoscale heterostructures. To address the large dimensionality of these time-domain quantum control fields, we introduce a gradientinformed directional subspace optimization (DSO) strategy that adaptively projects the problem into low-dimensional subspaces defined by gradient-derived directions. Within this framework, both standard BO and sparse axis-aligned subspace BO (SAASBO) are employed using Gaussian process surrogates with gradient information and Expected Improvement acquisition functions. Compared to traditional gradientbased line search methods, the BO-DSO and SAASBO-DSO techniques demonstrate faster convergence, improved sample efficiency, and more physically realistic control fields with reduced oscillatory behavior. Overall, this work demonstrates that combining Bayesian optimization with gradient-informed subspace expansion provides an effective and scalable solution to high-dimensional quantum optimal control problems in realistic quantum materials and devices.

item.title: A Water-Stable Zn(II)-H8-BINOL Metal-Organic Framework for Enantioselective Fluorescence Sensing
item.description: Chiral metal-organic frameworks (CMOFs) are attractive platforms for enantioselective fluorescence sensing, yet few CMOFs are capable of chiral discrimination in water. Water stability for enantioselective fluorescent sensors is particularly important given their potential applications in disease detection and environmental monitoring where analytes are in aqueous environments. We report the first H8-BINOL MOF capable of enantioselective fluorescence sensing in pure aqueous media. Enantiopure H8-BINOL-derived dicarboxylate MOFs were prepared and structurally characterised by single-crystal X-ray diffraction revealing that the structure adopts a similar structure to IRMOF-1 with a Zn4O(CO2)6 secondary building unit and the primitive-cubic (pcu) topology. The extended, hydrophobic H8-BINOL linker enforces a threefold-interpenetrated structure, which together with the steric shielding of the Zn4O node by the H8-BINOL backbone, enables water stability of the MOF for up to five days, a marked improvement over the hydrolytically sensitive parent IRMOF-1. In aqueous fluorescence measurements, native amino acids were excluded from the confined pores and gave no enantioselective response; the corresponding amino-acid ester derivatives in which zwitterion formation and the associated aggregation are suppressed were quenched enantioselectively with cysteine methyl ester and aspartic acid dimethyl ester. High enantioselectivity was achieved in water, with enantioselective ratio (er) of up to 23.9 for cysteine methyl ester and 6.0 for aspartic acid dimethyl ester. Notably, both host enantiomers preferentially recognised the same analyte enantiomer rather than opposite ones. This non-inversion of enantioselectivity is retained even in purely aqueous media and is incompatible with recognition at a discrete chiral centre and indicating enantiodiscrimination governed by the confined chiral pore environment.

item.title: Scale-Controlled Evaluation of Exact Molecular Assembly Index and Compression Baselines Across 626,131 Natural Products
item.description: The Molecular Assembly Index (MA), a core observable of Assembly Theory, quantifies the minimal number of recursive subgraph-joining operations required to construct a bond-labeled molecular connectivity graph. Recent critiques from algorithmic information theory contend that MA collapses to standard 1D string dictionary compression or Shannon entropy rates. Here, we evaluate 695,133 natural product structures from the COCONUT 2.0 repository using deterministic tree-nauty canonicalized branch-and-bound enumeration (assembly-theory==0.6.1) alongside a legacy C++ assemblycpp-v5 reference campaign across a 122-core local cluster, yielding 626,318 records flagged exact by the Rust workflow (is_exact = True) and a pinned completecase analysis cohort of 626,131 natural products (1 ≤ MA ≤ 36). Across 626,161 paired records with exact Rust results and valid C++ outputs, Rust and C++ indices correlate at r = +0.9674 (ρ = +0.9664) while achieving 57.20% (358,168) exact integer agreement (Rust < C++ in 249,243 pairs; Rust > C++ in 18,750 pairs), demonstrating strong rank association despite frequent integer disagreement across solver implementations and run configurations.

item.title: Chiroptical Photonic Manipulation in CdTe0.75Se0.25 Alloy Quantum Dots
item.description: Inducing chirality in intrinsically achiral semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) offers a promising strategy for developing functional materials for quantum photonics applications. Here, we demonstrate Zn-L-cysteine (ZnLC)-mediated chirality induction in achiral CdTe0.75Se0.25 alloy QDs. The experimental evidence suggests that ZnLC binds to tellurium (Te) and Selenium (Se) and modifies the local atomic environment and introduces structural asymmetry, leading to chirality in the system. Circular dichroism (CD) measurements reveal distinct chiroptical signatures in ZnLC-functionalized QDs. Such a chiral introduction is accompanied by substantial changes in photoluminescence dynamics, with fluorescence lifetimes reduced to ~160 times smaller than those of the achiral QDs. Single-particle fluorescence analysis demonstrates much improved photon emission with ON-fraction distributions reaching approximately 85-100% and a much reduction in fluorescence blinking statistics. Collectively, these findings establish ZnLC-mediated functionalization as an effective strategy for tailoring chirality to tune the emission dynamics for quantum photonic applications.

item.title: A machine-readable specification of the ISOS stability protocols, with protocol classification and refusing degradation metrics for perovskite photovoltaics
item.description: The ISOS consensus protocols define how accelerated stability tests on perovskite and organic photovoltaic devices should be run and reported, but they exist as prose and tables rather than as anything a machine can check. Two failures follow. Reported test conditions frequently do not determine a protocol designation, and the gap is usually one or two specific conditions that were never stated. Separately, the lifetime figure T80 denotes at least three distinct quantities, differing in which performance value is taken as the reference and when the clock starts, and published values are rarely qualified by which was used. We present isoskit, an open Python package that encodes 33 ISOS protocols as a versioned machine-readable specification with a JSON Schema, classifies a reported measurement into its protocol designation or names the conditions preventing designation, and extracts lifetime figures of merit under explicitly named reference conventions, returning a structured refusal wherever the reported measurement does not support extraction. Using the encoded specification we report three computational results. First, round-trip validation shows that 27 of 33 protocols are uniquely identifiable from their tabulated stress conditions; the remaining six form three degenerate pairs whose distinction lies in equipment and cycle profile rather than in stress conditions, one of which is induced by the encoding of inert-atmosphere humidity. Second, an exhaustive ablation over all 270,336 combinations of withheld conditions identifies six conditions without which no protocol in the set can be designated, and shows that withholding a single condition reduces the designated fraction from 81.8 % to 25.9 %. Third, on a two-phase ageing model the reference conventions diverge by a factor of 10.4 at a burn-in depth of 25 %, while linear interpolation of the crossing time remains accurate to 2 h at a 400 h measurement interval for which the defensible bracketing uncertainty is 400 h. The package is MIT licensed, has no runtime dependencies, and generates its own reference documentation from the specification.

item.title: Directing-Group-Driven Intramolecular [2+2] Photocycloaddition Catalyzed by Chiral-at-Metal Rh(III): Divergent Assembly of Oxa-, Thia-, Aza-, and All-Carbon Tricyclic Cyclobutane Scaffolds
item.description: Chiral polycyclic cyclobutane‑embedded architectures are privileged motifs in bioactive natural products and pharmaceutical candidates, yet general catalytic platforms to assemble heteroatom‑diversified tricyclic cyclobutane frameworks remain rare. Herein, we disclose an intramolecular enantioselective [2+2] photocycloaddition catalyzed by a chiral‑at‑metal Rh(III) complex via bidentate‑directing‑group‑assisted N,O‑chelation. Unlike conventional photocycloaddition manifolds relying on triplet‑energy transfer or charge‑transfer activation, stereochemistry‑defining N,O‑chelation preorganizes substrate geometry around the chiral metal center in the ground state before photoexcitation. Photoexcitation takes place on the intact catalyst‑substrate chelate complex rather than free substrate; no intermolecular energy transfer or charge‑separation processes operate, and intersystem crossing proceeds within the chelate to confine triplet‑state reactivity inside the chiral coordination sphere. This renders high‑fidelity stereochemical induction independent of the substrate’s intrinsic chromophore properties. Under blue‑light irradiation, the reaction furnishes chiral tricyclic cyclobutanes with up to three stereocenters (including one quaternary stereocenter), affording excellent diastereoselectivity (>20:1 dr) and enantioselectivity (up to >99 % ee). This unified catalytic platform enables divergent synthesis of four tricyclic classes: oxa‑, thia‑, aza‑, and all‑carbon cyclobutane skeletons, a capability unattainable with prior organocatalytic or Lewis‑acid‑based photocycloaddition protocols. The method tolerates electronically diverse aryl rings, various heteroaryl directing groups and other functional substituents. Importantly, gram‑scale synthesis is achievable at unchanged catalyst loading with full retention of yield and stereopurity, highlighting its practical utility for building large chiral polycyclic compound libraries for biomedical screening.

item.title: Head-to-tail cyclization of a peptide using a tethered homopolymer as a docking station for ring-closing and its extension to peptide synthesis and cyclization in the low bulk with mm-long tethers
From Self-Driving Laboratories to Connected Experimentation in the Physical Sciences: Lessons from the Critical Materials Value Chain
item.description: Self-driving laboratories close the loop between prediction, synthesis, and measurement on individual platforms, yet most physical-science research outside user facilities proceeds through multistage workflows distributed across separate laboratories, with manual handoffs of samples, protocols, and data. This review assesses how autonomous experimentation can extend across such workflows, using the critical minerals and materials value chain for energy technologies as a use case. The chain is a demanding test: dilute, heterogeneous feedstocks require characterization, separations, and materials synthesis performed in different laboratories with different instruments and safety bases. For capabilities demonstrated across U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories and the international literature, the review distinguishes closed-loop optimization from fixed-design screening, reports acceleration with explicit denominators, and identifies where human intervention remains. It examines what prevents single-site capabilities from compounding across laboratories: missing interlaboratory evidence for key measurands, unqualified handoffs of physical samples, and unassigned decision rights. These constraints are not specific to critical materials; they arise wherever bench-scale physical science spans sites. Building on published federated-experimentation frameworks, the review outlines a qualification profile for cross-site handoffs and closes with research needs in fundamental science, computing and verification infrastructure, and process development, each paired with a milestone and measure of success.

item.title: 4-Pyridylidene Bisiminothiolate Nickel Complexes as Structural and Functional Models of the Enzyme-Bound Nickel Pincer Nucleotide
item.description: Lactate racemase (LarA) and a recently discovered family of hydride transferases use the nickel pincer nucleotide (NPN) cofactor to shuttle a hydride to and from their substrates. The 4‑pyridylidene SCS pincer ligand of this cofactor is proposed to accept the hydride at the C4 position through a proton-coupled hydride transfer (PCHT) mechanism. Herein, we report a series of SCS nickel complexes supported by N-alkyl secondary thioamide pincer ligands (R = adamantyl, benzhydryl) as structural and functional models of this metallocofactor. Metalation with NiI2 affords an inseparable mixture of the monomer (H1SCSR)NiI, which carries an unsymmetrical thioamide/iminothiolate donor pair, and the neutral trimer [(SCSR)Ni]3, in which both arms are iminothiolates. Coordinating bases convert both species to the fully deprotonated adducts (SCSR)Ni(L) (L = N-benzylimidazole, NBIz; 1,1,3,3-tetramethylguanidine, TMG). The NBIz complex reproduces the C,S,S,N(imidazole) donor set and square planar geometry of the histidine-bound NPN cofactor, and its electronic absorption features are reminiscent of those reported for LarA. DFT calculations locate the LUMO on the pyridylidene ring with substantial density at C4. In combination with TMG, (SCSR)Ni(NBIz) catalyzes the racemization of lactic acid and related α-hydroxy carboxylic acids (TON up to ca. 8), and in situ studies identify (SCSR)Ni(tmg) as the resting state with no evidence for lactate coordination to nickel. Treatment with NBu4BH4 generates new absorptions comparable to those of the reported 1,4- and 1,2-dihydropyridinate complexes and of NaBH4-treated LarA, consistent with hydride addition at the C4 and/or C2 positions. Overall, these results align with a ligand-centered PCHT pathway and extend the racemization activity of synthetic NPN models from thiocarboxylate to thioamide-derived SCS pincer ligands.

item.title: Surface-Modified Ferrite Nanoparticles for Potential Magnetic Hyperthermia Cancer Therapy: A Comparative Heating Study in Water and Agar Phantoms
Assessment of machine-learned vs. classical/quantum atomistic simulations for predicting palladium-hydrogen materials
item.description: Palladium-hydrogen materials are used in a wide range of hydrogen storage, purification, sensing, and catalysis technologies; however, accurately predicting the structural and kinetic behavior of palladium hydrides remains computationally challenging. In this work, we present the first systematic assessment of Meta’s Universal Model for Atoms (UMA), a machine-learned interatomic potential, by benchmarking its predictions against density functional theory (DFT) and two widely used embedded-atom method (EAM) potentials for PdHx systems. All approaches were in close agreement for predicting equilibrium structural and thermodynamic properties, such as lattice constants and cohesive energies. In contrast, simulations of nonequilibrium hydrogen diffusion kinetics revealed substantial differences among the methods. Both EAM potentials predicted qualitatively incorrect hydrogen diffusion kinetics, exhibiting nearly instantaneous diffusion dynamics regardless of temperature and failing to capture the formation of molecular H2. UMA correctly reproduced the temperature dependence of hydrogen diffusion and qualitatively matched the DFT-predicted kinetic behavior, although diffusion timescales remained faster than DFT, particularly at lower temperatures. Overall, UMA provides the best balance between predictive accuracy and computational efficiency for large-scale palladium-hydrogen simulations, with DFT serving as a supporting role to obtain more accurate estimates of kinetic timescales, if needed. Our results show that existing EAM potentials (which were historically the most widely used atomistic methods for large-scale studies of these systems) should be used with caution, particularly for palladium-hydride diffusion kinetics.

item.title: Distance-Controlled Spin-State Inversion in Luminescent Donor-Bridged Trityl-Diradicals
item.description: We report a series of donor-bridged tris(2,4,6-trichlorophenyl)methyl (TTM) diradicals designed to elucidate how the radical-radical distance affects their spin coupling and luminescence properties. Electron-donating carbazole- and indolocarbazole-derived bridges link two persistent TTM radicals, while systematically increasing the distance between their radical centers from approximately 0.7 to 1.1 nm. All compounds exhibit pronounced diradical character y0 and charge-transfer-dominated optical transitions, yet their spin ground state depends sensitively on the bridge architecture. Whereas Cz2-TTM2 displays a near-degenerate singlet-triplet ground-state manifold, IdCz-TTM2 favors a singlet ground state with ΔEST,exp = −6.0 K. Further reduction of the radical-radical distance in Id2-TTM2 inverts the state ordering, and stabilizes the triplet relative to the singlet, resulting in a triplet ground state with ΔEST, exp = +2.5 K. The results show that subtle changes in the relative position and orientation of two TTM radicals can switch the ground state multiplicity of donor-bridged diradicals. This distance-dependent approach provides a molecular design strategy toward stable, luminescent triplet diradicals for optically addressable molecular quantum materials.

item.title: Evaluating cofolding methods for protein–macrocycle structure prediction
item.description: The accuracy of general-purpose cofolding models in predicting binding poses for novel protein–macrocycle complexes with little experimental structural precedent remains poorly characterized. We developed MacroCycle-Benchmark, which links chemically verified ligand structures to their experimental binding poses and protein environments across 1,861 cases. We evaluated six general-purpose cofolding models on a common set of 1,772 cases. With ligand SMILES as input, 22.7–30.8% of top-ranked predictions had a ligand heavy-atom root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) <2 Å after binding-site superposition and a local distance difference test score for protein–ligand interactions (LDDT-PLI) >0.8. Success rates were 10.7–16.5 percentage points lower for complexes released after each model’s training cutoff than for those released earlier. Among post-cutoff cases with evaluable similarity to pre-cutoff benchmark structures, all six models had success rates below 8% in the lowest-similarity group. In paired comparisons of cyclic peptides that could be represented by residue sequences and covalent linkages, Boltz-2 and RoseTTAFold 3 each recovered more experimental binding poses with sequence input than with SMILES. For macrocycles with 30–40 ring atoms, 97.5–100% of each model’s failed top-ranked SMILES predictions had a ligand heavy-atom RMSD of at least 2 Å even after ligand-only superposition. In these cases, the models failed to recover the bound conformation of the ligand itself, limiting their ability to reproduce the experimental binding mode. These findings indicate that current cofolding models have limited ability to generalize to macrocycle binding modes with little structural precedent in the benchmark. Predicted poses for such complexes should be used cautiously in structure-guided macrocycle design.

item.title: A Light-Driven Molecular Pump for the Active Transport of Non-Photoactive Organic Cations
item.description: Ion pumps transport charged species across biological membranes against concentration gradients, yet the active transport of organic cations by artificial systems remains largely unexplored. Light is an appealing energy source for driving such non-equilibrium processes and has been successfully employed to pump small inorganic ions. Here, we report a light-driven molecular pump that actively transports non-photoactive organic cations against their concentration gradient across a macroscopic liquid membrane. Key to pump operation is the use of a hydrogen-bonded azo-macrocycle that forms stable ternary complexes with organic dicationic cargoes, enabling their extraction from an aqueous phase into an organic phase. Upon irradiation, photoisomerization of the macrocycle weakens host-guest interactions and triggers cargo release into a second aqueous compartment. This light-controlled capture-transport-release cycle generates kinetic asymmetry and drives directional transport, leading to the buildup of macroscopic concentration gradients. This work establishes photoresponsive macrocycles as a supramolecular platform for converting light energy into the active transport of non-photoactive organic cations, providing a basis for macroscopic-scale applications.

item.title: Homoleptic ruthenium(II)-N-heterocyclic carbene complexes with metal-to-ligand charge transfer phosphorescence lifetimes up to 11 μs
item.description: [Ru(tpy)2]2+ (tpy = 2,2’:6’,2’’-terpyridine) and its derivatives are weakly emissive or non-emissive with extremely short metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) lifetimes. [Ru(tpy)2]2+ possesses a 3MLCT lifetime of about 0.25 ns. Herein we report a series of homoleptic Ru(II)-N-heterocyclic carbene (Ru(II)-NHC) complexes ([Ru(LH)2](PF6)2, [Ru(LPhMe2)2](PF6)2, [Ru(LPhOMe)2](PF6)2, and [Ru(LNaph)2](PF6)2) which are structurally analogous to [Ru(tpy)2]2+, however, display phosphorescence in deaerated acetonitrile solution at room temperature with record 3MLCT lifetimes up to 11.2 μs which is longest among any homoleptic Ru(II) complexes reported to date. Transient absorption spectroscopy and time-dependent density functional theory calculations have unambiguously supported these results. The homoleptic Ru(II)-NHC complexes possess higher 3MLCT state energies (2.35-2.58 eV) compared to both benchmark [Ru(bpy)3]2+ (bpy = 2,2’-bipyridine, 2.13 eV) and [Ru(tpy)2]2+ (2.07 eV) complexes, and their polypyridyl derivatives. They have been used as photosensitizers in challenging visible light induced [2+2] cycloaddition reactions, and dearomative cascade catalysis via energy transfer processes. Such photoreactions have not been accessible previously by using benchmark [Ru(bpy)3]2+ photosensitizer or its derivatives.

item.title: Synthesis of Chiral Tertiary Propargylic Alcohols by Using Dual Catalytic Activity of Halohydrin Dehalogenases
Best Practices in the Quantification of Electrochemically Regenerated 1,4-NADH: Can One Rely on Enzymatic Assays?
item.description: The accurate quantification of electrochemically regenerated 1,4-NADH is essential for evaluating the performance of the electrochemical regeneration process. Although enzymatic assays coupled with UV–Vis spectroscopy are widely used for this purpose, their reliability in distinguishing NADH isomers (1,4-NADH and 1,6-NADH) remains questionable. In this study, we investigate the limitations of the lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)-based enzymatic assay by comparing its results with those obtained using HPLC coupled with UV–Vis detection. Our findings reveal a significant discrepancy between the two analytical methods, demonstrating that the enzymatic assay can overestimate 1,4-NADH selectivity. This overestimation is attributed to the ability of LDH to interact with and consume the alternative 1,6-NADH isomer, thereby compromising the accuracy of the assay. These results highlight the importance of chromatographic separation for reliable quantification of NADH isomers and accurate determination of product selectivity during electrochemical NAD+ reduction. The findings also emphasize the need to carefully consider analytical methodology when evaluating the performance of electrochemical cofactor regeneration systems.

item.title: Ultra-High Density Pt Single-Atom Catalyst with Precisely Controlled Local Structure for Efficient Hydrogen Production
item.description: The precise control of coordination environment and increasing surface density of metal single atoms on oxide substrates, as well as improving their intrinsic activity for more efficient catalysis, remain significant challenges. In this work, we demonstrated how to modulate surface defects of commercial CeO2 support and investigated their influence on the local coordination environment and surface density of Pt single atoms (Pt1), which in turn impacted the catalytic performance in H2 production from methanol (CH3OH) decomposition. Our findings revealed that Pt single-atom catalysts (SACs) on CeO2 with Pt loading up to 15 wt.% could be successfully fabricated using defective Ce(OH)x support and a facile incipient wetness impregnation method. Through adjusting the defects in CeO2 supports, Pt/CeO2 SACs with distinct local coordination environments could be obtained. In CH3OH decomposition, the catalytic efficiency and stability of these Pt/CeO2 SACs were significantly influenced by the coordination environment of Pt1 species. Specifically, the Pt1 sites embedded within the CeO2 (110) lattice, forming a Ce-substituting square-planar Pt1O4 configuration, exhibited superior activity and stability compared to the surface adsorbed Pt1O4 sites. Systematic experimental and theoretical studies revealed that the abundant oxygen vacancies and weak binding with *H species on Pt/CeO2 catalyst with embedded Pt1 sites facilitated the adsorption of CH3OH and H2 desorption from the surface, thereby contributing to the enhanced CH3OH decomposition activity. These findings offer valuable insights into the fabrication of efficient SACs with ultra-high loading and optimal active sites for targeted reactions.

item.title: How to Publish Five-Star Battery Data
item.description: Battery research and development generates large amounts of diverse data, yet much of it is difficult to reuse outside its original context. This is due in part to the complexity of modern data management and the specialist knowledge needed to implement it. We introduce Five-Star Battery Data, an adaptation of the Five-Star Open Data scheme that presents a step-by-step pathway to publishing battery data on theweb. The five stars describe data that is published online under an open license, structured, serialised in open formats, annotated with ontology terms, and linked to related resources. For each star, we describe what it requires, how to implement it with existing open infrastructure, andwhat it enables. To demonstrate the framework in action, we present three case studies from different stages of the battery value chain. We first demonstrate integration with a robotic battery materials screening platform at Empa. We then show industrial relevance with examples from development of 100Ah prismatic cells at MORROW Batteries and testing of 745 cells at Microsoft. A worked example traces one test record through all five stars, one query over the three deposits leads from their metadata to their data, and an accompanying online course provides hands-on training.

item.title: Continuous-Flow Microreaction Resolves the Coupling Kinetics and Multistage Formation Mechanism of Hydrogen-Substituted Graphdiyne
item.description: Hydrogen-substituted graphdiyne (HsGDY) powder forms through alkyne coupling, network assembly, precipitation, and aging, yet the relationship between these processes remains poorly resolved. Here, a continuous-flow microreactor was combined with batch synthesis to investigate the process and mechanism of HsGDY formation in solution. Controlled flow residence times of 2–20 min access early network formation, whereas batch reactions follow subsequent evolution over 40–480 min. Complementary characterizations reveal rapid terminal-site consumption, slower conjugated-diyne maturation, and extended aggregate and pore development. A common infrared reaction coordinate links the two reactors and supports a formation pathway from oligomer coupling and network formation to micropore maturation. Ex-situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) identifies a 5–10 min structural window at 70 ◦C. The 10 min flow product exhibits a surface-carbon envelope comparable to that of the 360 min batch product but only 5% of its micropore volume, demonstrating decoupled chemical and pore maturation. The representative flow product delivers 107.4 F g−1 at 1 A g−1 and retains 103% of its initial capacitance over approximately 5000 cycles. Combining continuous-flow and batch synthesis thus reveals distinct time scales of HsGDY formation and connects reaction history with network structure and function.

item.title: Bayesian Hamiltonian Inference of the Oligoyne-Cumulene Transition in Linear Carbon Chains
item.description: Recent work on carbyne (the 1D carbon allotrope, linear carbon atomic chains) fragments Cn (𝑛 = 4 − 16) revealed an oligoyne-to-cumulene transition beyond a critical length (𝑛 ≥ 12). While a d-𝜋* backbonding mechanism was proposed to understand the observed behaviour, the cause of this threshold remained open. To explore this, we apply Bayesian inference to a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model of Cn single-molecule junctions, sampling the parameter space via dynamic nested sampling conditioned on experimental current-voltage characteristics. This Hamiltonian learning protocol delivers experimentally parameterised transmission spectra and allows insights into the transition mechanism. Although backbonding is significant as we originally postulated, the oligoyne-to-cumulene transition is smooth, and it’s cumulenic convergence at 𝑛 = 12 − 16 combined with interfacial coupling symmetrisation that drives the conductance increase into a length-independent regime. These findings provide a framework for extracting transmission spectra from experiment, unlocking a pathway toward effective Hamiltonian parameterisation to bridge quantum transport equations, experimental data, and chemical intuition.

item.title: Hybrids of 4-cyano-2-aryl-1,3-oxazole-5-sulfonamides with a 3-phenyl-1,2,4-oxadiazole motif: rational design, synthesis, in silico profiling, and antiproliferative activity against HepG2, A549, T98G, and HeLa human cancer cell lines
item.description: Multi-target anticancer agents attract growing interest for overcoming resistance and improving selectivity. Hybrids combining 1,2,4-oxadiazole and 1,3-oxazole scaffolds may target multiple oncogenic pathways simultaneously, yet the structural determinants of their activity remain poorly defined. Fourteen 1,3-oxazole/1,2,4-oxadiazole hybrids were designed, synthesized, and tested against HeLa, A549, HepG2, and T98G cancer lines, with non-cancerous NCTC clone 929 for selectivity. Two series were prepared: acyclic-linked hybrids (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12; –(CH2)n–, n = 2-7) and piperidine-linked analogs (13, 14). Activity depended steeply on linker length, peaking in compound 12 (n = 7), the most potent derivative (HeLa CC50 = 14.73 ± 2.02 µM; A549 CC50 = 43.92 ± 3.71 µM; HepG2 CC50 = 394.95 ± 24.01 µM; SI = 8 toward HeLa). Compounds 13 and 14 were inactive. Analysis of molecular geometry and electronic structure across the –(CH2)n–, series suggests compounds 2, 4, and 6 cannot engage productively with protein active sites: their tweezer-like geometry directs electron density into intramolecular contacts rather than outward-facing interactions. Lengthening the linker in 8, 10, and 12 shifts the geometry toward a more linear arrangement. Docking predicts interaction with the E6AP-binding pocket of HPV18 E6, with compound 12 occupying it at ΔG = –9.0 kcal/mol, consistent with the pronounced sensitivity of HPV18-positive HeLa cells. Virtual profiling implicated stress-response signaling (ARE, MMP, ATAD5) and aromatase. Compound 12 showed very low similarity to ChEMBL bioactives (p ≤ 0.3) and low predicted target-interaction probability, suggesting a potentially unrecognized mechanism. Linker length thus emerges as the principal determinant of antiproliferative activity in this hybrid class, defining compound 12 as a lead for HPV-associated cancers, with activity hypothesized to disrupt the oncogenic E6-E6AP interaction.

item.title: Interfacial Electronic Regulation and In-Situ Dynamic Reconstruction in a Bifunctional Composite Electrocatalyst for Efficient Overall Water Splitting
item.description: Developing efficient bifunctional electrocatalysts for overall water splitting is essential for sustainable hydrogen production in alkaline media, yet achieving both high activity and long-term stability remains challenging. Herein, we report a bimetallic NiFe metal-organic framework (MOF)-derived catalyst embedded in a conductive carbon matrix, which, upon pyrolysis, forms a NiFe-based phase with abundant interfacial active sites. The optimized NiFe@C catalyst exhibits excellent bifunctional performance, requiring overpotentials of 115 mV for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and 265 mV for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) at 10 mA cm-2, approaching benchmark Pt/C (96 mV for HER) and outperforming IrO2 (302 mV for OER) under identical conditions. The enhanced activity is attributed to synergistic interactions between Ni and Fe sites, the conductive carbon support, and interfacial electronic modulation, which facilitate intermediate adsorption and charge-transfer kinetics. In a conventional two-electrode configuration, NiFe@C || NiFe@C requires 1.79 V to reach 10 mA cm-2. In an anion exchange membrane (AEM) electrolyzer, the system delivers 200 mA cm-2 at 2.02 V and maintains stable operation for 100 h. In-situ and mechanistic investigations reveal reaction-dependent structural evolution. Under HER conditions, the catalyst remains largely structurally preserved, whereas under OER conditions it undergoes in-situ reconstruction toward an active NiFe oxyhydroxide phase that serves as the catalytically active phase for oxygen evolution. These findings highlight the synergistic roles of NiFe active sites, interfacial engineering, and dynamic reconstruction in enhancing bifunctional electrocatalysis for alkaline water splitting.

item.title: New mechanistic insights into electrocatalytic CO reduction from a bimodal parameter optimization strategy
item.description: Electrocatalysis stands at the cornerstone of our sustainable energy landscape. Yet, the search for better catalysts hinges on mechanistic understanding, which relies heavily on approximate quantum chemical techniques such as density functional theory (DFT). In this work, we acknowledge the error of DFT when modeling molecule–catalyst (metal) interactions by introducing formal error bounds to our calculated formation energies and to literature kinetic barriers. These data are further augmented by literature adsorbate–adsorbate interaction parameters and our electric double layer corrections for a complete picture of electrocatalytic kinetics. The resulting error-aware set of DFT data then informs a Bayesian optimization protocol with a sensitivity filter, reducing the remaining variance in the kinetic parameters by fitting to experimental steady-state electrochemical polarization curves. Because the model is built as a differentiable reaction system, its degrees of rate control are obtained by automatic differentiation. We apply this bimodal optimization protocol to electrochemical CO reduction on copper, representing a viable route for reduction of greenhouse gases and production of green chemicals and fuels. We show that our model can reduce the mechanistic hypothesis space by showing, e.g., that C–C coupling happens via the *CO adsorbates rather than atomic carbon, and it points to missing physics at high CO pressures, such as multiple site types or CO transport near the active sites. Our bimodal strategy balances theoretical and experimental insights, paving the way toward a new mechanistic understanding and catalytic design concepts for next-generation electrolyzers.

item.title: Computational Drug Discovery of Natural Product Compounds for Tyrosinase Inhibition
item.description: Plants produce chemically diverse compounds for defence and survival, many of which exhibit biological activity and offer promising starting points for drug discovery. This study thus investigated natural compounds as potential inhibitors of tyrosinase, a key enzyme in melanin production and an established target in the treatment of hyperpigmentation. A quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) machine-learning model was developed using ChEMBL tyrosinase bioactivity data and property-matched decoys. Ten models, including decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting, were evaluated; logistic regression was selected for virtual screening. To make the model generalise to unseen chemistry, the model was tested on compounds that were required to have Tanimoto similarity of 0.40 or less to every training compound and to share no Bemis–Murcko scaffold with them. The model achieved an AUC of 0.82 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.78–0.86), compared with 0.56 using physicochemical properties alone. The frozen model was then used to screen 404,570 natural products from COCONUT (COlleCtion of Open Natural prodUcTs) and IMPPAT (Indian Medicinal Plants, Phytochemistry And Therapeutics). Of the top 1% of predictions, 1,694 compounds were both structurally novel and represented new scaffolds. Following computational filters for predicted skin permeability and potentially reactive chemical groups indicating skin irritation, the 100 highest-scoring candidates were selected for molecular docking. Docking reproduced the crystallographic tropolone binding pose with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 1.20 Å, while the most predictive docking score achieved an AUC of 0.64 (95% CI, 0.61–0.66). Among the ten highest-ranked candidates, two were associated with Anisomeles indica (Indian catmint) and two with Phaseolus lunatus (lima beans). These candidates warrant experimental validation and further investigation for potential dermatological applications.

item.title: Tunable Oxygen Evolution Activity on the Lanthanum Oxide Terminated Perovskites
item.description: Electronic structure descriptors have been widely used to predict the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity. Herein, the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) is used to predict active LaO-terminated LaBO3 (B = Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu) perovskites for the OER. Density functional theory calculations show that the adsorption free energies of ∗O on La–La sites are correlated with the HOMO. In contrast, the Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni and Cu sites of the BO2 termination show a weaker dependence on the HOMO. Changes in the magnetic moment show that the La–La sites are non-oxidisable, so the electrons are taken from the surrounding perovskite. The B sites are oxidisable and provide the electrons locally. Comparing the theoretical overpotential with the HOMO, a volcano-type trend is shown for the La–La sites, which is not observed on the B sites. A composition-based model predicts active LaO-terminated LaCo1−xCuxO3. Finally, a correlation is shown between the experimental OER overpotentials from three independent studies in the literature and the computed HOMO.

item.title: A Versatile (Photo)Electrochemical Array with Temperature, Illumination and Mass Transport Control for Measurements from Molecules to Microorganisms
item.description: The growth in (photo)electroactive materials development creates a demand for platforms that can systematically measure and compare (photo)electrochemical reactions. Existing electrochemical screening platforms offer limited control over experimental parameters and the range of samples that can be assessed. Here, we developed a versatile multi-well electrochemical array platform that offers programmable control of illumination, temperature, and convection. The platform incorporates a programmable stage that automates plate positioning and electrode washing to minimize cross-contamination between measurements. The sample plates can accommodate customizable electrodes and have been designed to fit into plate readers, allowing complementary optical analyses. Eight wells are measured simultaneously, and the full plate (with 24-wells) is screened in three successive rounds. Electrochemical consistency across the array was validated by cyclic voltammetry of [Fe(CN)6]3−/4−, with 0.13% carryover between successive measurements. Reproducible chopped-light photocurrents were obtained from the photoactive molecules [Ru(bpy)3]2+ and methylene blue under different LED wavelengths and calibrated light intensities. Lastly, currents from the photosynthetic cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 were measured across a large range of conditions, including applied potential, temperature, stirring, and mediator concentration, to systematically identify the conditions for optimal photocurrent output. Notably, parallel electrochemical mediator screening was completed in one day, compared with an estimated 12 days for the sequential workflow. This study establishes a much-needed analytical platform that reproducibly generates high-quality photoelectrochemical data from diverse photoactive materials, accelerating the discovery of high-performance systems.A multi-well (photo)electrochemical array with programmable control of illumination, temperature, and convection, enables parallel and reproducible measurements of samples ranging from electroactive molecules to living photosynthetic microorganisms.

item.title: CertMat: Formally Certified Robust Phase and Elastic Stability Verification Across One Million Inorganic Crystals
item.description: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) and high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) workflows have expanded candidate inorganic crystal catalogs to the million-material scale, yet thermodynamic convex hull stability (Ehull = 0) and mechanical Born stability (C ≻ 0) remain evaluated almost exclusively via floating-point point estimates that neglect energy and stiffness uncertainties. Here we introduce CertMat, an exact rational certificate generator and machine-checked Lean 4 formal verification kernel (leanprover/lean4:v4.16.0, zero Mathlib dependencies, zero sorry or non-standard axioms across 51 mechanized theorems) that certifies worst-case phase and elastic stability over heterogeneous uncertainty boxes. CertMat mechanizes four core theorem families: (1) exact Farkas primal-dual soundness with non-negative margin enforcement (δ ≥ 0) for convex hull decompositions, (2) exact algebraic cancellation of correlated elemental reference-state errors ( ∑ e cieδµe) proving that only uncorrelated residual errors (ηi) can flip phase stability, (3) universal worst-case interval robustness over heterogeneous energy boxes Ei ∈ [Li, Ui] with an exact Charnes–Cooper linear-fractional solver for the critical destabilization radius ε∗(x) and adversarial decomposition Phase Switching, and (4) exact rational LDLT Born positive-definiteness, constructive non-PD strain counterexamples, Voigt Frobenius–Weyl robustness and constructive rank-1 fragility witnesses, and bidirectional pure-rational SO(3)-invariant Mandel/Kelvin Frobenius–Weyl robustness and constructive rank-1 fragility theorems (requiring no irrational √ 2). Auditing 1,044,460 unique crystal phase entries (plus 234,086 matched PBE–r2SCAN sub-hull re-audits, totaling 1,278,545 competed LP audits and 1 uncompeted elemental phase) and 34,323 valid 6 × 6 elastic tensors across Google DeepMind GNoME (PBE and r2SCAN), NIST JARVIS-DFT 3D, and Matbench Discovery WBM—with 95,348 / 95,348 serialized TSV rational certificates machine-verified by the compiled Lean 4 certmat-check binary and an independent pure-Fraction checker (0 failures) plus 540/540 stratified spot-audit dataset-binding checks—we establish four major findings: (i) on 117,043 matched GNoME PBE-vs-r2SCAN crystals, correlated elemental shifts explain R2 = 73.51% of formation-energy discrepancies (reducing MAE from 78.90 to 30.96 meV/atom), and CertMat’s worst-case Fragile classification separates real r2SCAN stability flips with 24.65x relative risk (0.46% vs. 11.36% flip rate, ROC-AUC 0.8948) on exact 117k matched sub-hulls and 5.10x relative risk (96.40% recall) on GNoME’s primary external Decomposition Energy Per Atom column (6.20x relative risk / 97.46% recall on ... MP); (ii) 11,481 of 34,323 (33.45%) valid JARVIS-DFT 3D elastic tensors fail exact Born stability with Lean-certified rational strain witnesses, while 2,643 (11.57%) of Born-PD crystals are fragile under unconstrained 5 GPa Voigt perturbations (Lean-certified via WEYL_FRAGILE) and 1,517 (6.64%) are fragile under SO(3)-invariant 5 GPa Mandel perturbations (bidirectional Lean certification: 22,531 MANDEL_ WEYL_ROBUST + 3,198 MANDEL_WEYL_FRAGILE witnesses); (iii) 19,894 of 42,688 (46.60%) WBM candidates reported stable against the static MP2020 hull collapse to strictly unstable under intra-catalog WBM competition alone (62.19% via same-composition polymorphs, 37.81% via cross-composition decomposition; 40.80% even after unique-prototype deduplication); and (iv) our exact hull audit uncovered a pervasive upstream unit-scaling defect in the published NIST JARVIS-DFT 3D Figshare release (jdft_3d-9-24-2025.json) consistent with dividing per-atom optb88vdw_total_energy a second time by reduced formula-unit atom count Nfu, inflating ehull > 1.0 eV/atom for 63,386 materials (median residual 0.00677 eV vs. 2.605 and 2.108 eV for two negative controls). Code, Lean 4 proofs, and full verification artifacts are publicly available at https://github.com/sunpunggi1/certmat.

item.title: Nonempirical Double-hybrid Functionals Entering the AI Field: the Adaptative LS1DH model
item.description: We introduce a machine-learning-assisted nonempirical double-hybrid density-functional approximation, dubbed adaptative LS1DH or aLS1DH, which combines the theoretical constraints of the linearly scaled one-parameter double-hybrid (LS1DH) model with system-specific flexibility. Based on kernel ridge regression (KRR) and convolutional many-body distribution function (cMBDF) representations, aLS1DH predicts optimal system-dependent fractions of nonlocal exchange and correlation while preserving size consistency. Its performance is assessed on the extended GMTKN55 and on the recently developed CYCLO70. The aLS1DH model consistently improves upon its parent functional, PBE0-DH, rivaling the latest machine-learning-based functionals such as skala functional. These results highlight the potential of machine learning to improve the accuracy of nonempirical double hybrids while retaining their underlying theoretical constraints.

item.title: Chemistry decides the calibration unit: five direct and one water-mediated interaction class
item.description: Typed protein–ligand contact models predict which interactions form, but they return point probabilities, not a statement of how often the true contact is included. We formulate per-atom, multi-label interaction sets for five direct contact classes (H-bond, hydrophobic, π, salt, halogen) and add water as a sixth, water-mediated class. Using cross-conformal calibration and conformal risk control on 750 crystal complexes across 29 targets, we show that the calibration unit is a chemical decision rather than a statistical default. At the 90% nominal level a chemistry-aware nonconformity score reduces set size by 7.9% (target-held-out) and 13.2% (scaffold-held-out), changing coverage by only +0.6/−0.6 percentage points. Per-type risk control attains false-negative rates of 0.096/0.079 at a 10% target, but only for classes with enough calibration positives: salt has 42 positives and is not estimable, while π is under-covered by a global threshold. Water is abundant (1,258 positives; 5.4% of ligand heavy atoms; 72% of complexes) and target-specific. A global threshold on the probability score leaves water at 0.905/0.937/0.931/0.853 coverage on target/scaffold/temporal/strict splits, but the original chemistry-aware score is water-blind by construction and drops to 0.735/0.751/0.750/0.635. Making the partner term water-aware recovers only 0.848/0.877/0.886/0.787, while per-type control gives 0.923/0.937/0.928/0.857. Per-type control is therefore not a universal winner: it fixes π and water, can lower halogen, and cannot estimate salt. The calibration unit should follow the chemistry of the class, not an aggregate coverage target.

item.title: When Nondetects Decide the Verdict: Left-Censored Data Handling and Compliance Decision Errors under Extreme Censoring
item.description: Compliance assessments commonly replace nondetects with zero, half, or the full reporting limit. We asked how often this choice, not the data, determines whether a 95th percentile (P95) or mean exceeds a regulatory limit. In a pre-specified simulation spanning 20–99% nondetects, structural zeros, and 30–1000 samples, we evaluated decision errors of substitution, nonparametric, censored-likelihood, and Bayesian methods. With one reporting limit, lower- and upper-bound substitution rarely disagreed at ≤80% nondetects but in 53–61% of data sets at 95% when the reporting limit exceeded the regulatory limit. In a screening reanalysis of the Fifth Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR 5), substitution alone determined whether 458 PFOA and 406 PFOS systems were classified as exceeding maximum contaminant levels at the reporting limit. In simulations of this case, lower-bound substitution missed exceedances despite more sampling. In exploratory analyses, no eligible method kept both error rates ≤20% with 30 samples for most nondetect proportions. For upper-limit decisions, the best method needed roughly 300–400 samples at ≤95% nondetects, largely reflecting the narrow decision margin, and none sufficed with up to 1000 at 99%. Under extreme censoring, data often cannot identify the decision. The remedy is more samples or lower reporting limits, not a better estimator.

item.title: Downstream purification route influences the viscoelastic properties of silk-elastin-like polypeptide hydrogels
item.description: The development of novel recombinant protein-based materials requires a bottom-up understanding of sequence-processing-property relationships. However, most studies have focused on how the amino acid sequence determines material properties, whereas the effect of downstream purification (DSP) remains largely unexplored. Here, we compare two silk-elastin-like polypeptides (SELPs) with different molecular weight (MW) and clustering of silk-like blocks. Each SELP was purified by two different DSP routes: inverse temperature cycling (ITC) or ammonium sulfate precipitation (ASP). Using a combination of experiments and molecular simulations, we show that the DSP route affects hydrogel formation and viscoelastic properties in a sequence-dependent manner. The low MW SELP was insensitive to the DSP route, whereas ITC of high MW SELPs led to irreversible hydrogel formation and with a 2-fold higher storage modulus than ASP. Our multiscale characterisation suggested that DSP influences how readily silk-like blocks form intermolecular βsheet crosslinks as a function of the DSP route. These results indicate that SELP hydrogel properties can be modulated not only by sequence design, but also through the DSP route applied, which has implications on cost and efficiency for designing scalable SELP biomanufacturing processes.

item.title: Learning to Smell: Representing Olfaction with Artificial Intelligence
item.description: Olfaction plays a fundamental role in how humans perceive and interact with their chemical environment, yet predicting how odors are perceived remains a major scientific challenge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced odor prediction, but its capabilities depend critically on how chemical and perceptual information is represented and learned. In this review, we examine how different molecular representations shape both the predictive capabilities and scientific insights of AI models for olfaction. We discuss the progression from predefined molecular descriptors to learned representations and biologically anchored models incorporating odorant receptor information, highlighting what each approach can capture and where its limitations lie. We further examine challenges in predicting complex odor mixtures, concentration-dependent responses, and individual differences in perception, as well as the scarcity and heterogeneity of experimental data. We propose data integration and biologically informed representation learning as opportunities to improve generalization and help connect molecular recognition with olfactory perception. Finally, we argue that future progress should be measured not only by predictive accuracy but also by AI models' ability to generate experimentally testable insights into the mechanisms of olfaction.

item.title: Accurate, Rapid, and High-Throughput Photophysical Determination of Critical Micelle Concentrations of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances
item.description: Aggregation is a defining yet poorly characterized physicochemical behavior of many per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), influencing their environmental fate, interfacial partitioning, and treatment performance. Critical micelle concentration (CMC) is a key physicochemical parameter describing PFAS aggregation; however, CMC data remain limited, and existing measurement approaches are often labor-intensive, PFAS-consuming, low-throughput, or dependent on specialized instrumentation. Here, we develop and validate a photophysical assay for PFAS CMC determination leveraging microplate reader technology. The assay provides three independent yet consistent readouts, fluorescence emission, UV-vis absorbance, and fluorescence polarization, enabling robust CMC determination with minimal sample consumption. Using perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) as a model compound, the assay yielded CMC values in excellent agreement with conventional conductivity and 19F NMR measurements. Application of the assay to a diverse set of PFAS revealed the influence of molecular structure and head-group chemistry on aggregation behavior. Temperature-dependent measurements further demonstrated chain-length-dependent micellization trends, while environmentally relevant solution conditions showed minimal effects of natural organic matter but pronounced impacts of ionic strength, cation valency, and PFAS mixture composition. Together, these results provide systematic experimental evaluation of PFAS aggregation behavior, revealing how PFAS species and environmental chemistry govern micellization while establishing a scalable platform for PFAS physicochemical characterization.

item.title: All-Optical Nuclear Spin Hyperpolarization via Spin Level Anti-Crossing of Pentacene Transient Triplet State
item.description: We demonstrate all-optical nuclear spin hyperpolarization in pentacene-doped naphthalene single crystals via the spin level anti-crossing (SLAC) of photoexcited triplet states. Using pulsed laser excitation alone without microwave irradiation, we obtain a bulk 1H polarization of ∼0.4% at 80 K near the SLAC (∼12.5 mT), corresponding to an enhancement of ∼ 2.5×104. The polarization arises from state mixing driven by the zero-field splitting and hyperfine interactions in the laboratory frame. The magnitude and orientation of the field tune the energy gap between the two triplet sublevels at the SLAC. For molecules aligned with the field, this gap can match the nuclear Larmor frequency, analogous to the solid effect (SE) in dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP). Misalignment can widen the energy gap beyond the nuclear Larmor frequency at all fields, in which case polarization arises from state mixing analogous to resonant-mixing (RM) DNP. The unexpected field profile is explained by a small distribution of molecular orientations. We further show that magnetic-field modulation synchronized with the laser pulses increases the polarization and accelerates its build-up similar to the integrated solid effect. These results establish an efficient, robust and microwave-free route to nuclear hyperpolarization and all-optical control of electron-nuclear spin systems.

item.title: Beyond Shape: Odorant Conformational Ensembles Encode Topology, Molecular Size, and Polar-Surface Coherence
item.description: Odor is widely modelled as three-dimensional shape recognition: a flexible odorant presents a 300 K conformer ensemble to a receptor repertoire, implying that perceptual breadth peaks at an intermediate number of accessible shapes and that explicit 3D representations outperform 2D molecular graphs. We test both predictions under a cryptographically pre-registered plan across catalogue profiles (n = 4,808), human psychophysics (n = 304) and heterologous receptor arrays (n = 294). Computing 300 K GFN2-xTB ensembles at a 200-conformer ceiling for all 1,821 flexible cohort members (106,526 conformers) and benchmarking 21 neural representations across 10 seeds, we find that neither claim holds. Conformational entropy saturates by 28 conformers (88% attained at a ceiling of 20), excluding an interior breadth optimum sixfold below the populated range (β2 = +0.0080, 95% CI -0.0014 to +0.0172). No 3D representation outperforms a capacity-matched or descriptor-augmented 2D graph. Out-of-sample-replicated confound analyses show that 3D shape dispersion vanishes once chain topology is controlled; instead, breadth reflects coarse topological flexibility (peaking at 9.2 rotatable bonds), molecular extent and polar-surface coherence (concave β2 = -0.0264). Keywords: conformational ensemble · odor breadth · molecular representation · Artificial Intelligence · Graph Neural Network

item.title: A Foundation Model for Accurate Atomistic Simulations in Drug Design
item.description: Artificial intelligence has revolutionized the prediction of static protein structures, but characterizing their dynamics and their interactions with drug candidates remains a computational bottleneck. Simulations that address this challenge need both the accuracy of quantum chemistry and the speed to reach biologically relevant timescales. To meet these requirements, we introduce FeNNix-Bio1, a fast and scalable foundation machine-learning potential trained primarily on high-accuracy quantum chemistry data, which enables reactive atomistic simulations of biological systems. Here, we show that FeNNix-Bio1 captures subtle condensed-phase phenomena such as ion solvation and the properties of liquid water, predicts the hydration free energies of more than 600 small molecules and the absolute binding free energies of 30 protein-ligand complexes in good agreement with experiment, and describes protein structure and dynamics, lipid bilayers and chemical reactions, in simulations of up to more than a million atoms.

item.title: Boltz-GenFree: structure-generation-free ranking for first-stage affinity screening
item.description: Boltz-2 predicts affinity from a structure it generates for every candidate, which makes library-scale screening expensive, and several studies suggest that this pose contributes little to the predicted affinity. We tested this with fine-grained interventions and built Boltz-GenFree, which predicts affinity without building a structure for any candidate, generated or docked. On its own it keeps 90% of the Boltz-2 mean AP, against 67% for Boltzina, and combined with Boltz-2 in a simulated two-stage screen, in which only the top 10% of its ranking is re-ranked, it matches the mean AP of Boltz-2 alone on eight libraries (0.0839 against 0.0840) at an estimated 8.5 to 8.9 times lower cost. Its cheap ranking can thus decide where to spend the expensive steps, whether the shortlist re-ranked by Boltz-2 or the 300 labels used for fine-tuning, which raised AP on seven of eight targets.

item.title: 4-Pyridylidene Bisiminothiolate Nickel Complexes as Structural and Functional Models of the Enzyme-Bound Nickel Pincer Nucleotide
item.description: Lactate racemase (LarA) and a recently discovered family of hydride transferases use the nickel pincer nucleotide (NPN) cofactor to shuttle a hydride to and from their substrates. The 4‑pyridylidene SCS pincer ligand of this cofactor is proposed to accept the hydride at the C4 position through a proton-coupled hydride transfer (PCHT) mechanism. Herein, we report a series of SCS nickel complexes supported by N-alkyl secondary thioamide pincer ligands (R = adamantyl, benzhydryl) as structural and functional models of this metallocofactor. Metalation with NiI2 affords an inseparable mixture of the monomer (H1SCSR)NiI, which carries an unsymmetrical thioamide/iminothiolate donor pair, and the neutral trimer [(SCSR)Ni]3, in which both arms are iminothiolates. Coordinating bases convert both species to the fully deprotonated adducts (SCSR)Ni(L) (L = N-benzylimidazole, NBIz; 1,1,3,3-tetramethylguanidine, TMG). The NBIz complex reproduces the C,S,S,N(imidazole) donor set and square planar geometry of the histidine-bound NPN cofactor, and its electronic absorption features are reminiscent of those reported for LarA. DFT calculations locate the LUMO on the pyridylidene ring with substantial density at C4. In combination with TMG, (SCSR)Ni(NBIz) catalyzes the racemization of lactic acid and related α-hydroxy carboxylic acids (TON up to ca. 8), and in situ studies identify (SCSR)Ni(tmg) as the resting state with no evidence for lactate coordination to nickel. Treatment with NBu4BH4 generates new absorptions comparable to those of the reported 1,4- and 1,2-dihydropyridinate complexes and of NaBH4-treated LarA, consistent with hydride addition at the C4 and/or C2 positions. Overall, these results align with a ligand-centered PCHT pathway and extend the racemization activity of synthetic NPN models from thiocarboxylate to thioamide-derived SCS pincer ligands.

item.title: AtomTrans: A Plane-Wave-Based Computational Platform for Electron and Phonon Quantum Transport with Atom-Anchored Wannier Functions
item.description: We present AtomTrans, a computational platform for coherent electron and harmonic phonon transport based on plane-wave density-functional theory. AtomTrans combines systematic control of the plane-wave basis with atom-labelled Wannier functions for open-boundary calculations. Projectability-guided disentanglement selects the electronic subspace, and Löwdin orthonormalization of projected atomic trial orbitals yields atom-labelled Wannier functions. Electrode blocks extracted from device buffers share a common gauge and energy reference with the scattering region. AtomTrans applies the same partitioning scheme and Green’s-function solver to the electronic Hamiltonian and an independently calculated dynamical matrix. The software calculates transmission, total and projected densities of states, real-space local density of states, and thermoelectric coefficients. Finite-bias currents are evaluated using either the fixed equilibrium transmission or a self-consistent electrostatic treatment. Comparisons with QuantumATK cover three representative systems. For an Au–benzenedithiolate–Au junction, we examine molecular resonances, spatial distributions, and the current–voltage response. Compared with the rigid-transmission approximation, electrostatic self-consistency reduces high-bias current deviations from QuantumATK. The relative deviations are at most 3.1% at ±1.8 and ±2.0 V. For an armchair graphene nanoribbon, phonon thermal conductances agree within 4% at 300–900 K, and both software packages yield a peak thermoelectric figure of merit of 0.19 at 300 K. For an Au–Co–Au chain, the minority-spin antiresonance is highly sensitive to the LCAO basis, whereas increasing the plane-wave cutoff from 400 to 800 eV shifts its position by only 0.01 eV. These results demonstrate AtomTrans’s capabilities for charge and heat transport and illustrate the systematic control of plane-wave basis convergence in spin-dependent transport.

item.title: Transition-Metal-Free Amination of Aryl Halides via Facile Aryne Generation
item.description: Despite continued advances in transition-metal-catalyzed amination of aryl halides, persistent challenges, including costly scale-up, sensitivity to steric hindrance, and catalyst poisoning by heteroaromatic rings, necessitate the development of metal-free alternatives. Aryne intermediates are an attractive option due to their high reactivity, yet facile aryne generation from aryl halides remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we disclose a transition-metal-free amination strategy for aryl halides that uses KHMDS with an 18-crown-6 additive, proceeding via aryne intermediates. The reactions use exclusively commercial reagents, proceed at room temperature, and achieve near “dump-and-stir” simplicity for reaction setup. The methodology is applicable to a wide range of aryl and heteroaryl halides with excellent chemoselectivity, including (S)-3,3′-dibromo-2,2′dimethoxy-BINOL and strongly Lewis basic substrates such as quinoline and pyrimidine that typically impede Pd-catalyzed aminations. Both primary and secondary amines participate, including sterically hindered 1-adamantylamine and diisopropylamine, providing a basis for preparative scale synthesis and evaluation of medicinally relevant aryl halides and amines.

item.title: Influences of Surface Reconstruction and Iron-Associated Activation of Nickel-Based Electrocatalysts on Oxygen Evolution Reaction
item.description: Ni-based electrocatalysts are among state-of-the-arts for oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in alkaline media, and their interaction with Fe impurities in the electrolyte is widely understood as an origin of the enhanced catalytic performance. The surface of these catalysts undergoes physicochemical changes in electrochemical operation environments, and this reconstruction of surface is intertwined with the Fe-associated promotion of activity. However, these two phenomena have often been understood together, and their influences were difficult to be comprehended separately. Herein, we used SrNiO3 and LaNiO3 as model catalysts with different surface-reconstruction behaviors. By examining their characteristics in the absence and present of Fe in the electrolyte, importance of the access to Fe species in the electrolyte could be unveiled. Based on systematic investigations, we then found out that the interaction between the Fe and the catalyst surface under active reconstruction (during the initial stage of operation) might lead to a negative contribution to the overall OER activity. To resolve this issue, we suggest a simple strategy to maximize the catalytic performance; inducing the surface reconstruction in the absence of Fe, followed by exposure of the catalyst to Fe in the electrolyte for the promotion of OER. Around two-fold increase in the performance were achieved in optimized conditions, though identical catalysts were used, and the versatility of our approach was verified by applying the same strategy to Ni hydroxides.

item.title: Superhydrophobic Surfaces Across the Agri-Food Continuum: Mechanisms, Multifunctional Antifouling, Water-Saving Operations, and Sustainable Pathways from Pre-Harvest to Post-Harvest Systems
item.description: Interfacial fouling across agricultural production and food processing drives foodborne illness, post-harvest spoilage, excessive water and chemical consumption, and energy losses. Superhydrophobic surfaces—characterized by static water contact angles exceeding 150° and sliding angles below 10°—offer a unifying physical and chemical defense across the pre-harvest to post-harvest continuum. This review critically evaluates advances predominantly from 2023 to 2026 in superhydrophobic and wetting-engineered coatings targeting bacterial biofilms, fungal spores, soil and mud adhesion, viscous liquid food residues, thermal dairy fouling, and pipeline drag or scaling.
