item.title: A Perturbed Bismuth(0) Atom with a J = 3/2 Ground State
Active Gold Unmasked: Sum-Frequency Generation Reveals the Premonolayer Oxidation of Low-Coordination Sites
item.description: Low-coordination gold atoms are thought to oxidize long before the surface oxide forms and to control its electrocatalytic activity, yet their oxidation leaves no clear voltammetric signature and has been inferred only indirectly. Here we detect it with sum-frequency generation (SFG), which probes the metal itself rather than the current. On polycrystalline gold at pH 9, SFG resolves a second population that oxidizes inside the double-layer region, where the voltammogram shows only cation adsorption. It removes an additional ~20% of the SFG intensity and is lost with first-order kinetics over successive cycles, even between 0.4 and 0.6 V vs SHE, until cathodic pretreatment regenerates it. First-principles calculations on four gold facets show that the oxidation onset follows coordination and identify this population with the seven-coordinated step-edge atoms of Au(211), which oxidize about 0.3 V before the Au(111) terraces, forming hydroxyl layers rather than hydrous Au(III) oxide. At pH 9 these atoms stay hydroxylated throughout cycling and relax into the lattice, the deactivation long proposed for metastable active gold; at pH 1 they oxidize with the terraces. The approach can likewise track low-coordination active sites on other metal electrodes, such as platinum and copper, under working conditions.

item.title: One Interface, Five Geometries: An Open-Source Python Toolkit for Visualizing Wavefunctions in One-, Two-, and Three-Dimensional Infinite Potential Wells
item.description: The infinite potential well is the first quantum model students solve in closed form, and most software for it stops at one dimension. The two-and three-dimensional wells carry the concepts students find hardest: degeneracy, its symmetry origin and its lifting by anisotropy, and the topology of nodal lines and surfaces. We present the Infinite Potential Well Visualizer (IWV), an open-source Python toolkit with a Tkinter interface that treats five geometries in one workflow: the one-dimensional box, the two-dimensional rectangle, the three-dimensional box, the disk and the sphere. Each state is evaluated analytically, reported in joules and electronvolts, and rendered in six plotting modes, from line plots and heatmaps to interactive Plotly volumes. Because all geometries share one interface, one energy scale and one set of conventions, students can compare the degeneracy of a square well with its lifting in a rectangle, or the Bessel structure of the disk and sphere with the trigonometric structure of the box. We describe the physics, the numerical treatment of Bessel zeros, the visualization layer and measured performance; a 3000× 3000 grid is evaluated in 0.27 s. Every figure here is unedited output of the program’s own plotting functions.

item.title: Assessing the Stability, Synthesizability, and Transport Properties of Aliovalently-Doped Multivalent Solid Electrolytes
Graded, not all-or-none: single-cell Raman reveals antifungal suppression in Candida
item.description: Heavy-water (D2O) labelling with single-cell Raman spectroscopy is becoming a basis for rapid antifungal susceptibility testing, but its read-outs are usually population means or the share of cells above a cut-off. Neither can tell whether a drug slows every cell (graded suppression) or stops some cells while others continue (all-or-none suppression). We reanalysed 10,348 public single-cell spectra from eight Candida strains exposed to amphotericin B (AmB), flucytosine (5-FC), micafungin (MCF) and voriconazole (VOR). Two-state mixtures anchored to unlabelled cells were fitted to the C–D label distributions, and graded, switch, free and null dose-series models were compared by BIC. The graded model was preferred for 15 of 27 series, including 5-FC in all five tested strains; across five robustness variants only one graded series moved clearly to a model with off cells. Coexisting off and labelled cells at one dose were robust only for AmB in C. glabrata 368 and MCF in C. krusei. In simulations built from the observed cells, a cut-off classifier reported a uniformly dimmed population at 20 % of control as 20 % “active” cells, whereas the mixture recovered the fully labelled population; a fully active minority of 5 % was detected in 88–98 % of simulated datasets. Label build-up saturated within the assay window (k = 0.37–0.58 h 1), so end-point labels understate rate - suppression. Distribution-level analysis, rather than cut-offs, is needed before Raman read-outs are interpreted as numbers of active or tolerant cells.

item.title: Neural Network Representations of Diphenalenyl Molecules for Property Prediction
item.description: Predicting magnetic and electronic properties of molecular systems from their structure is essential for the design of molecular qubits. In this work, we present a hybrid neural network architecture combining Directed Message Passing Neural Networks (D-MPNN) with a Transformer, to predict the magnetic exchange coupling J and polarizability P of substituted diphenalenyl molecules. We generated a dataset of halogen-substituted diphenalenyls (F, Cl, Br, I) at 16 positions using Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations. The generated data have then been employed to develop a deep neural network architecture to predict the properties of interest. Our approach encodes both the molecular graph topology through message passing on directed edges and the sequential nature of chemical substitutions through attention mechanisms. The unified encoder combines graph-level representations with positional and substituent embeddings, enabling accurate multi-task prediction of J and P.

item.title: Hierarchical Theory of Chemical Bond: From the Schrödinger Equation to Aromaticity and Homochirality
item.description: Chemical bonds are described by many complementary concepts whose relationships and limits are often unclear. Building on the four empirical directions of two-center bonding identified by machine learning in the preceding article, we formulate a hierarchical theory of the chemical bond from the electronic Schrödinger equation. Because the energy is an exact functional of the one- and two-particle reduced density matrices, partitioning these matrices among fragments (atoms, functional groups, or molecules) organizes bonding information by the connectivity of the fragments and by its kind: one-particle coherence, electron correlation, or response. Two-fragment quantities (bond index, covalent–ionic coordinate, bond polarity, and π fraction) describe bond multiplicity and polarization, whereas correlated bond cleavage separates the loss of electron sharing from the growth of static correlation, and hydrogen bonding and dispersion are distinguished by their coherence and cumulant signatures. Three-center delocalization is determined by pair blocks of the density matrix, but maximum-entropy calculations reveal three-orbital correlation beyond all pair information. Ring delocalization likewise differs from aromatic response: current-coupled excitations govern aromaticity, Baird reversal, and the collective response of fused rings. Finally, an exact expansion over all 64 stereoisomers of two hexaalanine helices attributes 99.9% and 98.6% of the variance of their energies to one-residue fields imposed by a helix of fixed handedness, a quantitative form of the principle of chirality hierarchy. Each level of the hierarchy is thus defined by the information that the levels below it do not contain.

item.title: Neighbor-Graph Truncation and Density Shift in Equivariant Direct-Hessian Potentials: Diagnosis, Controls, and Mitigation
Predicting the Host-guest Binding Gibbs Free Energy for Guests
item.description: Host-guest chemistry involves noncovalent interactions between host and guest molecules and has been applied in areas such as adaptive materials, sensing, and drug delivery. However, the discovery of new hosts and the identification of suitable guests remain challenging because selective binding is governed by subtle and often competing noncovalent interactions that are difficult to predict. To overcome this predictive limitation, computational framework was developed to predict Gibbs free energies of host-guest binding using a hybrid machine-learning model. The model was trained and tested on 4155 host-guest systems manually curated from the literature and combines descriptors derived from semiempirical quantum-mechanical calculations with three-dimensional molecular fingerprints. Evaluation on a test set yielded an R2 of 0.83 and a mean absolute error of 3.1 kJ per mol. The computational efficiency of the model enabled prediction times of approximately one to five minutes per host-guest system with an average size of 174 atoms, supporting the framework’s applicability to high-throughput screening for host-guest discovery.

item.title: Self-Driving Laboratory for the Optimization of Coacervate Morphology and Cargo Partitioning
item.description: Engineering coacervates as functional compartments requires control over both droplet morphology and the molecules they recruit; yet coupled, nonlinear interactions make the required formulations difficult to predict. Here, we present a self-driving laboratory (SDL) that combines automated multi-component formulation, confocal microscopy and quantitative image analysis with Gaussian-process-based optimization to connect desired properties to experimentally accessible formulations. Within predefined campaigns, each set of measurements guides the next experiments, allowing the SDL to identify both optimal properties and extended regions compatible with a requested response. Specifically, the SDL reproducibly maximizes mean droplet diameter and identifies formulations predicted to yield specified mean sizes. Varying electrolyte composition maps changes in particle density, while protein-additive experiments identify formulations that resist wetting in both polypeptide and synthetic polyelectrolyte coacervates. Additionally, the SDL measures cargo in the dense and dilute phases to guide optimization of apparent partitioning, using sample volumes 100-fold smaller than those used for bulk validation. These measurements reveal how favorable formulations depend on cargo charge and multivalency, with enrichment trends supported by independent bulk measurements of selected formulations. These results establish autonomous property optimization as a practical and effective method for engineering coacervate morphology and cargo partitioning.

item.title: Kinetically Regulated Aqueous Co-precipitation and Extended Hydrothermal Crystallisation of Cobalt Magnesium Carbonate (Mg Co )CO Nanoparticles: Thermodynamic Feasibility, ₁₋ₓ ₓ ₃ Ethylene Glycol Coordination, and Prospective Applications
item.description: Cobalt magnesium carbonate, (Mg Co )CO , was synthesised by an ethylene-glycol- and ⁺ CTAB-assisted aqueous co-precipitation route followed by extended hydrothermal crystallisation at 250 °C for 16 h. The synthesis was designed around the thermodynamic feasibility of carbonate precipitation and the kinetic challenge arising from the different precipitation tendencies of Co²⁺ and Mg² . Ethylene glycol was incorporated to modify Co² coordination and regulate its availability ⁺ during co-precipitation, while the extended hydrothermal residence promoted crystallisation and structural development. Powder X-ray diffraction shows the principal reflections of a calcite-type rhombohedral carbonate (R c) in both Sample 3 (pre-autoclave) and Sample 4 (hydrothermally 3̅ ₃ processed). Local fitting of the composition-sensitive (113) reflection gives centres of 42.8672° and 42.9176°, respectively; lattice-parameter interpolation gives apparent x(Co) values of approximately 0.72/0.42 using Graf end-member metrics and 0.60/0.35 using the independently reported Pertlik CoCO cell. FTIR identifies carbonate vibrational bands at and ν₃ ν₂ ⁻ ⁻ = 844.7 cm ¹ (S3) and 869.8 cm ¹ (S4), ⁻ = 1363.4 and 1386.6 cm ¹, respectively. SEM–EDX detects both Co and Mg at every analysed site, with mean cation fractions x(Co) = 0.483 (S3, n = 4) and 0.348 (S4, n = 5). These diffraction, vibrational and elemental-composition trends jointly establish the formation of cobalt magnesium carbonate and show that S3 is relatively Co-rich compared with S4. SEM reveals aggregated, locally faceted particles; UV–Vis spectra above 280 nm show the near-UV and broad visible absorption associated with the Co-containing carbonate; and DLS gives hydrodynamic diameters of 491 and 306 nm and PDI values of 0.314 and 0.053 for S3 and S4, respectively. The 16 h hydrothermal treatment is associated with a 37.7% reduction in hydrodynamic diameter and an 83.1% reduction in PDI across the recorded S3/S4 process histories. The work establishes a thermodynamically designed, kinetically regulated route to cobalt magnesium carbonate and discusses its relevance as a mixed metal carbonate precursor for oxide, catalytic, energy-material and carbon-mineralisation pathways.

item.title: Overcoming n–π* Transition Forbiddenness via Through-Space Conjugation
item.description: A long-standing challenge in organic luminescence is that the symmetry-forbidden nature of n–π* transitions imposes an intrinsic trade-off between long-wavelength emission and high quantum efficiency. Here we show that through-space conjugation (TSC) between heteroatom lone pairs can activate otherwise forbidden n–π* transitions, thereby reconciling these requirements. Using dipyridylmethane (DPyM) isomers with systematically varied nitrogen positions, we demonstrate that inter-nitrogen distance and excited-state conformation dictate the strength and nature of TSC. (o,o)-DPyM, with the shortest nitrogen–nitrogen distance, exhibits the longest emission (up to 530 nm) and the highest quantum yield among the isomers. Time-dependent density functional theory reveals that a coplanar syn conformation in the excited state elevates the HOMO through nitrogen–nitrogen TSC and activates the n–π* transition, simultaneously narrowing the energy gap and enhancing the radiative decay rate. Sterically constrained analogues and model compounds support the idea that this TSC-mediated n–π* activation is responsible for the red-shifted emission and enhanced efficiency. This work establishes a general design principle for converting forbidden transitions into efficient radiative pathways, enabling high-performance long-wavelength organic emitters.

item.title: Learning organometallic reactivity with a flow matching model for mechanism prediction
item.description: Organometallic chemistry is critical to front-line chemical discovery, and the development of new methods is driven by a strong understanding of reaction mechanisms. Data-driven mechanism prediction models are an emerging complement to experimental and first-principles mechanistic studies, but their coverage of organometallic reactivity is limited by scarce training data. In this work, we use mechanistic templates for 41 families, or unique transformations, of organometallic reactions to extract over 1.2 million organometallic mechanistic steps from patent literature. We trained a flow matching model for electron redistribution in organometallic chemistry (FlowER-OM) on this expanded dataset, reaching 97.6% top-5 step accuracy across a held-out test set spanning organic and organometallic chemistry. Without selectivity-specific training, the model reproduces known regioselectivity trends for several elementary steps. FlowER-OM recovers mechanistic pathways for unseen reactions, including sequential catalytic cycles and unseen coupling partners. Furthermore, only a few examples of new reactivity are required to fine-tune new classes of mechanistic steps, new metals, or correct erroneous selectivity predictions. We find that under-and overrepresentation of categories of reactivity lead to failure modes observed in selectivity, mechanistic path elucidation, and fine-tuning. FlowER-OM is a strong predictor of classic organometallic chemistry and recognizes broad reactivity patterns, while its limitations expose the boundaries of current mechanism prediction models and can help guide future dataset design.

item.title: Less is more in mixture modeling: every molecular vector is a map, yet the mixture is the territory
item.description: Predicting mixture properties remains a fundamental challenge in chemical informatics, yet most deep learning pipelines reuse the single-molecule recipe: they compress each molecule into a fixed-length vector before predicting the mixture's behavior. We argue that a molecule's intrinsic information is defined by two orthogonal components: its atomic dimensions (node-level features) and its topological connectivity (edge-level bonds). Non-injective pooling mathematically obscures the latter, forcing existing models to compensate through massive scale or exhaustive feature engineering. Here, we propose a direct modeling strategy: modeling the mixture directly as a unified atomic system with intact topology. Our instantiation, AtomFormer, preserves both atomic dimensions and connectivity with only 1.2M parameters and no pretraining. A simple implementation of this design achieves or approaches state-of-the-art baselines across diverse domains, demonstrating that the failures of existing vector-based models on certain tasks stem from the same root cause: every molecular vector is a map, yet the mixture itself is the territory.

item.title: Molecular Dynamics Assessment of Monomer-level Approximations in Density Functional Theory of Polymer Electrolytes: From Bulk to Ceramic Interfaces
item.description: Determining the interactions and chain or ion dynamics in the bulk polymer phase and at polymer-ceramic interfaces is crucial for next-generation polymer-ceramic composite electrolyte design, where polymer chain dynamics and interfacial structure strongly influence ion coordination and transport. In this work, we combine density functional theory (DFT) calculations and classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to investigate Li+ coordination and interfacial structure in poly(lithium sulfonyl (trifluoromethane sulfonyl)imide methacrylate) (pMTFSILi) and Li0.5La0.5TiO3 (LLTO) systems. Firstly, single chain and bulk polymer-only MD simulations are used to investigate the impact of chain length and tacticity in the MD structure build on ion coordination in the polymer. For these MD simulations of the polymer phase, it is shown that DFT polymer fragment approximations underestimate ion binding in the bulk, but that Li+ energetics are likely controlled by repeat unit chemistry as opposed to chain architecture and conformation, which is qualitatively captured in DFT models.Secondly, DFT calculations of monomer and dimer adsorption on LLTO surfaces are then done to establish reference interfacial geometries and local coordination environments. These DFT structures are used to validate the cross-interactions between polymer and ceramic atom types used in the classical MD simulations by comparing partial radial distribution functions, which exhibit a consistent first-shell coordination environment between DFT and MD. These indicate accurate reproduction of local interfacial chemistry by modeling these cross-interactions as mostly electrostatic (Coulombic-dominated). Thirdly, we build on this validation to perform classical MD simulations of an extended atomistic bulk polymer and LLTO interface to examine structural organization beyond isolated polymer fragment adsorption. The results of these simulations demonstrate that the validated MD interatomic potential, specifically the cross-interactions between the polymer and ceramic atom types, captures key features of Li+ coordination at the polymer-ceramic interface and enables extension from simplified polymer fragment adsorption models to realistic interfacial structures. The resulting multiscale framework thus provides a foundation for future atomic-scale computational studies on ion transport and interfacial dynamics in polymer-ceramic composite electrolytes.

item.title: Crucible Matters: Systematic Investigation of Flux-Mediated Al-Doped SrTiO3 Photocatalyst Synthesis
item.description: The flux-mediated molten-salt synthesis of Al-doped SrTiO3 (Al:STO) has produced the highest efficiency in the field of photocatalytic water splitting, yet lab-to-lab reproducibility and upscaling synthetic conditions have proven difficult. Much of this variability arises from underreported synthetic details, including reaction temperature, cooling rate, chemical supplier and composition, salt-to-precursor (S:P) ratio, crucible size and supplier, and synthesis batch size, all of which influence material structure and composition. Here, these often-overlooked parameters are systematically evaluated through comprehensive characterization and their effect on the photocatalytic degradation of the anionic dye methyl orange (MO). Optimized synthesis conditions (1100 ℃ flux temperature, 10 ℃ min-1 cooling rate, SrCl2·6H2O at a 5:1 S:P, 80 mL crucible, and 300 mg batch size) yielded highly active Al:STO with 0–20 mol % Al doping (k = 2.10 ± 0.24 h-1 for 20 mol %). Applying these conditions at the gram-scale, however, resulted in significantly reduced activity, prompting further analysis to explore correlations across synthesis and characterization variables. Both statistical and experimental findings identified the alumina crucible surface area-to-precursor chemical volume (prior to heating) ratio (SA:V) as the dominant predictor of activity, while added Al2O3 played a secondary role, contributing primarily through particle size suppression. The positive relationship between SA:V and MO degradation was mirrored in relative photocatalytic H2 evolution, suggesting that optimized synthesis parameters are relevant for predicting activity across a broad range of photocatalytic processes. These results demonstrate the high sensitivity of flux-mediated Al:STO synthesis to subtle variations in preparation parameters and provides a blueprint toward greater reproducibility in photocatalyst synthesis.

item.title: Compliance-Conditioned Molecular Generation Across Optical, Polymer, and Central Nervous System Targets with Graph Neural Network Ensembles
item.description: Generative molecular design usually optimises a single physical or biological target while treating regulatory bans and safety risks as an afterthought. At the same time, reinforcement learning against a single surrogate readily exploits out-of-distribution features or collapses onto narrow scaffolds. We evaluate a unified compliance-conditioned generation framework that embeds explicit regulatory and safety gates directly into REINVENT policy-gradient fine-tuning, guided by four-architecture 2D graph neural network ensembles (GINE, GATv2, MPNN, and CARATE) and audited by an independent ExtraTrees holdout excluded from training rewards. Across three distinct chemical domains on a single RTX 3060 GPU, the framework resolves domain-specific failure modes. For UV-Vis chromophores (400–450 nm), graph-ensemble rewards align training and holdout gains above 70% in-band yield across 3 seeds while cutting cross-seed variance nearly fourfold. For engineering polymers (Tg 450–550 K), where 15.07% of the curated corpus fails REACH or bisphenol-A rules, compliance-gated generation reaches 99.97% compliance with a fourfold increase in target-band yield. For non-hallucinogenic central nervous system ligands (5-HT1A versus cardiac 5-HT2B and hERG anti-targets), supervised warm-starting overcomes reward sparsity but triggers a selectivity trap that degrades cardiac safety. Smooth multiobjective safety fine-tuning paired with Bemis–Murcko scaffold memory resolves both cardiac safety and mode collapse, restoring uniqueness to 0.994. Finally, retrosynthetic audits confirm strong synthetic accessibility across all domains, and ab-initio TD-DFT screening on 50 UV-Vis candidates confirms visible absorption in 65.2% of converged structures while quantifying the residual surrogate-to-quantum gap.1

item.title: Building a grain-boundary machine-learning force field by reactive sampling and data curation, and its application to large-scale grain-boundary transport in Li6PS5X (X =Cl, Br)
item.description: General-purpose machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) achieve near-DFT accuracy for equilibrium properties, yet their reliability for rare, non-equilibrium events—such as Li migration in grain-boundary (GB) corescannot be judged from static error metrics alone. Here we present a datageneration, curation, and validation framework that turns this judgment into a routine check, demonstrated on argyrodite Li6PS5X. Reactive-path sampling (ODPMD) concentrated in the transition region yields configurations far from the existing data (44% novel vs. 4% for intact-phase frames), which are screened by a physical-consistency filter and selected by stratified sampling in a MatterSim descriptor space. Fine-tuning MatterSim on this compact, regime-balanced data set reduces held-out DFT Li-migration barrier errors from 44meV to 32meV MAE (median 25meV), mainly in the rate-limiting high-barrier tail, while retaining bulk properties. MD on GB models of up to 4344 atoms shows, for both models, a mild activation penalty (∆Ea = +50–80 meV) that suppresses Li diffusion mainly at low temperature (DGB/Dbulk ≈ 0.46 at 500 K vs. 0.59 for the universal model at the ordered boundary) but is nearly invisible at the 700–800 K commonly simulated; electric-field-driven non-equilibrium MD corroborates this weak blocking. The universal model thus captures the qualitative physics, but its quantitative reliability can be established only by validating local barri-

item.title: Free-Energy Population Optimization in Chemical Space: Spectral Dynamics and Product-of-Experts Molecular Generation
item.description: We formulate molecular design as optimization of a probability distribution p(x) over an accessible chemical space, regularized toward a reference distribution q(x) while enriching a molecular reward R(x); minimization yields the analytic target distribution p∗(x) ∝ q(x) exp[R(x)/τ ], with the effective temperature τ controlling the reward–regularization trade-off and the resulting distributional concentration. After validation in a one-dimensional toy system, application to a 24,994-molecule DRD2 data set showed strong reward enrichment, while reversible molecular-similarity-graph dynamics revealed metastable chemotypes, gateway molecules, and analogue corridors governed jointly by graph connectivity and molecule-specific stationary weights. We then applied the framework to molecules generated by prior, DRD2 expert, and Product-of-Experts (PoE) chemical language models: direct docking increased the DRD2+ fraction from 1.15% to 20.17% for PoE, and the empirical PoE docking-score distribution was closely matched by the variational family at τeff ≃ 1.41. These results show that the framework provides a common distributional description for interpreting chemical-space organization and calibrating molecular generators against an effective-temperature-parametrized target family.

item.title: Boltz-GenFree: structure-generation-free ranking for first-stage affinity screening
item.description: Boltz-2 predicts affinity from a structure it generates for every candidate, which makes library-scale screening expensive, and several studies suggest that this pose contributes little to the predicted affinity. We tested this with fine-grained interventions and built Boltz-GenFree, which predicts affinity without building a structure for any candidate, generated or docked. On its own it keeps 90% of the Boltz-2 mean AP, against 67% for Boltzina, and combined with Boltz-2 in a simulated two-stage screen, in which only the top 10% of its ranking is re-ranked, it matches the mean AP of Boltz-2 alone on eight libraries (0.0839 against 0.0840) at an estimated 8.5 to 8.9 times lower cost. Its cheap ranking can thus decide where to spend the expensive steps, whether the shortlist re-ranked by Boltz-2 or the 300 labels used for fine-tuning, which raised AP on seven of eight targets.

item.title: Distinct Pathways of Surfactant-Induced Membrane Destabilization: Experimental and Computational Insights into Adsorption, Permeabilization, and Solubilization
item.description: Surfactant-induced membrane destabilization involves adsorption, changes in membrane organization, permeabilization, and solubilization, processes that do not necessarily evolve in parallel. Here, we combine experiments and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to investigate anionic SDS, cationic DTAB, and nonionic C10EO8 interacting with neutral and negatively charged phospholipid liposomes under different ionicstrength conditions. ζ-potential, Laurdan generalized polarization (GP), calcein leakage, and dynamic light scattering were used to probe adsorption, local membrane organization, permeabilization, and vesicle disruption, respectively. SDS and DTAB adsorption was detected at concentrations far below their respective critical micelle concentrations (CMCs), with comparable apparent adsorption free energies but membranecharge-dependent saturation capacities. In contrast, large-scale vesicle disruption occurred predominantly near and above the CMCs. SDS produced a pronounced electrokinetic response but the slowest leakage, whereas DTAB caused nearly complete sub-CMC leakage while largely preserving the vesicular population. C10EO8 produced minimal sub-CMC GP changes yet permeabilized membranes one to two orders of magnitude faster than the ionic surfactants. MD simulations predicted increasingly favorable bilayer transfer from SDS to DTAB to C10EO8 and revealed distinct incorporation pathways: ionic surfactants exchanged predominantly via monomers, whereas C10EO8 transferred rapidly from micelles into bilayers and exhibited a lower flip-flop barrier. Together, these findings show that surfactant charge and individual membrane observables cannot independently predict membrane-disrupting behavior, highlighting the importance of integrating adsorption, membrane organization, leakage kinetics, and molecular insertion mechanisms.

item.title: Functional Upcycling of Waste PET towards Carbon-Based Hybrid Composites for Electromagnetic Interference Shielding
item.description: The growing prevalence of electronic devices is driving demand for reliable, lightweight electromagnetic shielding. In this study, a rational approach was proposed for upcycling preliminary recycled waste polyethylene terephthalate (PET) into lightweight carbonbased materials designed for electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding. The fabrication process involves forming MOFs (UiO-66 and Ni-BDC) on the surface of hydrolyzed PET-waste wafers, followed by laser-assisted carbonization using a 405 nm LED laser system to produce PET@C(Me) (Me = Zr, Ni) coatings. The different steps leading to the formation of PET@C(Me) were characterized using various techniques to assess the morphology, phase and chemical composition. The resulting composite coatings demonstrated EMI shielding efficiency above 99.37 % and 99.68 % for PET@C(Zr) and PET@C(Ni), respectively. Owing to the excellent performance of PET@C(Me) composites and a convenient upcycling strategy, this approach opens new avenues for preparing lightweight materials from plastic waste for EMI shielding in microelectronic devices.

item.title: Targeted Versus Broad Descriptor Generation: A Case Study in Primary Sulfonamide Acidity
item.description: As machine learning becomes increasingly common in chemistry, an important question is how chemical knowledge should guide molecular featurization. Here, a simple rule-based acidity score for primary sulfonamides was developed through the selection, encoding, and weighting of molecular features using open-access RDKit tools. Initial feature weights were assigned based on established chemical principles governing acidity and refined by comparison with a DFT-derived ranking of 44 compounds, achieving Spearman’s ρ = 0.779. Applied unchanged to an independent dataset of 32 experimentally measured pKa values, the score showed strong agreement with acidity rankings (ρ = 0.794, τb = 0.611) and compared favorably with QupKake, a machine-learning pKa estimator. These results suggest that simple structure-based descriptors can approximate DFT-and experimentally derived acidity trends without repeated quantum-chemical calculations. Further data-driven optimization of feature weights improved agreement with the DFT development data but worsened performance on the experimental dataset. A broader feature-generation approach employing 150 automatically generated RDKit descriptors likewise reduced performance on the experimental dataset. These findings highlight the broader potential of using established chemical principles to guide the development of simple, accessible, and interpretable molecular representations.

item.title: Which Chemical Priors Should Bayesian Optimization Trust, and How Strongly?
item.description: Bayesian optimization is transforming experimental discovery in chemistry, but its success depends critically on how chemical candidates are represented. While recent approaches emphasize flexibly adapting chemical representations on-the-fly based on experimental feedback, we investigate a complementary perspective: selecting a representation whose initial similarity relationships are well suited to the optimization task, and preserving these relationships unless experimental evidence warrants their revision. At a more fundamental level, we show how pretrained chemical representations, combined with appropriately calibrated Gaussian process hyperpriors, jointly establish chemically informed prior beliefs about the system under investigation. Through systematic benchmarking and analysis of representation geometries, we demonstrate that the choice of the underlying pretrained chemical representation substantially influences optimization performance, with the most effective representations varying across chemical domains. Notably, appropriately selected fixed representations can outperform approaches that explicitly adapt their embeddings throughout the optimization campaign, using a standard Gaussian process equipped with a dimension-aware hyperprior, without requiring explicit modification of the underlying embeddings. Our findings therefore highlight the importance of systematically characterizing the suitability of pretrained representations across different chemical optimization domains, with chemical intuition potentially providing additional guidance for their selection. More broadly, our approach offers a straightforward, practical and versatile means of incorporating chemically informed prior beliefs into Bayesian optimization.

item.title: Merging substrate permissive biocatalysis with chemical derivatization to build post-translationally modified lipidated peptides
item.description: Lipidation enhances the pharmacologically desirable properties of peptides and proteins. However, biocatalytic lipidation is often constrained by the enzymatic selectivity for the peptide and the lipid substrates. Here, we combine substrate-permissive biocatalysis with chemical derivatization to generate structurally diverse lipidated peptides. We demonstrate the use of promiscuous enzymes to install lanthionine crosslinks and azole heterocycles in peptide substrates, which subsequently undergo sequential diazotransfer and copper-mediated azide–alkyne cycloaddition to append lipid moieties. This workflow accommodates saturated, aromatic, heterocyclic, and fluorinated lipids and extends to chemically synthesized peptides, including head-to-tail macrocyclic peptides containing non-proteinogenic amino acids. Site specificity for chemical lipidation is controlled by the incorporation of lysine residues at any desired location, as well as enzymatic conversion of N-terminal glutamine to pyroglutamate. Efficient modification across lanthipeptides, linear azol(in)e-containing peptides, and head-to-tail macrocycles demonstrates compatibility with distinct peptide architectures. By decoupling peptide maturation from lipid installation, this modular chemoenzymatic strategy expands access to site-selectively lipidated, post-translationally modified peptides and provides a foundation for exploring how lipid identity influences peptide function.

item.title: Generation of triarylmethyl cations and oxygen nucleophiles from triarylmethanol derivatives for hydride-abstraction-mediated transformations
item.description: A method for hydride-abstraction-mediated transformations using triarylmethanol derivatives is disclosed. The generation of triarylmethyl cations and oxygen nucleophiles from triarylmethanol derivatives enables a range of transformations through hydride abstraction. In particular, acyl fluorides were synthesized from o-hydrosilyl-substituted benzotrifluorides with triarylmethanol derivatives via C–F cleavage.

item.title: Spherical Resolution for Fast and Rigorously Bounded Mixed-Precision Coulomb Integrals on GPUs
item.description: We present a formulation of the Coulomb matrix for graphics processing units (GPUs) in which the electron-repulsion integrals are evaluated by a spherical resolution instead of the common recursion formulae or Rys quadrature, and we show that it yields a rigorous bound of the rounding error of single-precision (FP32) arithmetic up to high angular momentum. Each Hermite Coulomb intermediate is resolved into a finite sum of radial functions multiplied by real spherical harmonics of the direction between the two Gaussian product centers. When this direction is rotated onto the z axis, only the m = 0 terms remain and the interaction of two Hermite densities becomes diagonal in the magnetic quantum number, while the rotation is a linear transformation of fixed dimension 2l + 1 that acts on two-index density and potential blocks. As a result, no intermediate depends on another, which removes the limit that recursion formulae encounter on GPUs at high angular momentum. In cc-pVQZ on one NVIDIA A100, the Coulomb calculation is up to 91 times faster than that of GPU4PySCF for the 28 molecules of Thiel’s benchmark set, and this ratio approaches 6–10 for larger systems with up to 12 500 basis functions. With respect to JoltQC, it is 6.4–15 times faster for small and large systems alike, and, with the present engine’s quartets screened at 10−10, it is 2.4–3.8 times faster than published EXESS computation times for 26 large systems. Because the evaluation separates into orthogonal rotations and a radial part, the FP32 rounding error of the ERIs of each primitive shell quartet evaluated in the local frame is bounded a priori. In all calculations examined, the FP32 error is much smaller than that of the Schwarz screening and is therefore of no consequence for the accuracy. item.title: Chloride Ions Enhance Sulfur Oxidation at the Air–Water Interface in Single Aqueous Aerosols
item.description: Multiphase sulfur oxidation in aqueous aerosols plays a significant role in haze pollution. We employ here an aerosol optical tweezer with cavity enhanced Raman spectroscopy to monitor the oxidation of dissolved S(IV) to S(VI) in single aqueous aerosols with radii of ~4 μm and examine the impact of chloride ions on sulfur oxidation rates. Our previous work showed that for aqueous aerosols of this size, the interfacial oxidation mechanism dominates the reaction kinetics, with rates over two orders of magnitude faster than the bulk reaction. We show here that the presence of chloride ions at an aerosol pH near 7 results in a further increase of over an order of magnitude in the interfacial oxidation rate, yielding a 104 enhancement in sulfate formation compared to bulk values. At higher pH, the impact of chloride ions is less pronounced. To account for these results, a synergistic effect whereby protons and chloride ions together at the interface is proposed to enhance dissolved S(IV) to S(VI) oxidation. A mechanism involving chloride ion reactions with sulfur oxide radical species at the interface is proposed to be the cause of the enhancement. A kinetic model parameterizing the chloride dependence of interfacial reactivity reproduces the observed kinetic trends and predicts rapid sulfate formation in submicron aerosols. As discussed here, this study reveals the role of chloride in accelerating interfacial S(IV) oxidation with protons present, which has the potential to exacerbate haze pollution in chloride-rich coastal regions.

item.title: Spacer accommodation under geometric confinement governs phase behavior in mixed Ruddlesden–Popper and Dion–Jacobson halide perovskites
item.description: Mixing organic spacers broadens the structural diversity of two-dimensional (2D) halide perovskites (HPs); however, predicting whether chemically distinct spacers can be incorporated into a shared layered phase remains a significant challenge. Here, we integrate high-throughput compositional screening and diffraction-based phase mapping with molecular dynamics simulations accelerated by machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIP-MD) to investigate combinations of five Dion–Jacobson (DJ) spacers with varying alkyl-chain lengths and three aliphatic or aromatic Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) spacers. Contrary to conventional structural-matching expectations, large differences in parent-phase interlayer spacings do not necessarily preclude spacer mixing, whereas smaller differences do not guarantee it. MLIP-MD simulations of locally mixed and phase-separated spacer configurations reveal a correlation between local d-spacing deviations relative to the parent DJ phase and experimentally observed phase behavior in aliphatic spacer combinations. The simulations further reveal that these trends arise from molecular accommodation within the geometric constraints imposed by the DJ framework, where RP and DJ spacers adapt their orientations and conformations to accommodate a shared interlayer geometry while preserving favorable intermolecular packing. Guided by these insights, selected mixed-spacer compositions that combine DJ interlayer bridging with RP conformational flexibility exhibit enhanced thermal and ambient stability, while mixed-spacer surface treatment of 3D HPs improves photovoltaic performance and thermal stability. Together, these findings establish molecular accommodation as a guiding principle for spacer selection beyond conventional structural matching, and provide a route toward predictive synthesis of layered HPs.

item.title: Correlating CO2 reduction selectivity with ML-quantified morphology of surface Cu and cracks in gas diffusion electrodes
item.description: Gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) enable Cu-catalyzed CO2 electroreduction (CO2RR) at industrially relevant current densities, but their porous, multicomponent architecture evolves during operation, affecting selectivity and stability in poorly understood ways. We use machine learning clustering of post-mortem electron micrographs to quantify the morphology of surface Cu and cracks of three types of copper-carbon paper GDEs at different stages of CO2RR selectivity decay. Pixels are grouped by lightness to identify bright regions associated with agglomerated or rough Cu catalyst and dark regions associated with cracks that extend through the Cu layer in the gas diffusion layer. For each class, we quantify the average patch area, average total area, and average boundary length. These descriptors correlate with C2H4, CO, and H2 Faradaic efficiencies at least as strongly as conventional observables such as electrode resistance and potential, and gas or liquid pressure. Larger average Cu patch areas correlate with lower C2H4 and CO selectivity in nanoparticle electrodes, consistent with detrimental nanoparticle agglomeration. In contrast, both larger average Cu patches and a larger total area of rough Cu correlate with higher C2H4 and CO selectivity in sputtered electrodes, consistent with a larger electrochemically active Cu surface area. Across electrode types, larger crack patches are associated with higher C2H4 and CO selectivity relative to H2, consistent with cracks providing preferential drainage pathways that limit flooding. Without a Nafion overcoat, larger crack patches combined with a smaller total crack area are associated with higher C2H4 and CO selectivity, whereas Nafioncoated electrodes retain selectivity despite more extensive cracking. Our findings identify morphological parameters that can guide the design of more selective and stable CO2RR electrodes.

item.title: Polymorphous Structural Landscapes Drive Broadband Optical Response in Water-Stable Mixed-Halide Antiperovskites
item.description: Silver chalcohalide antiperovskites have emerged as low-toxicity semiconductors with strong near-infrared absorption, although their unusual composition-dependent optical properties, including inverse bandgap bowing, remain poorly understood. Here, Ag3SI1-xBrx solid solutions were synthesized by a solvent-free mechanochemical route and investigated by structural and optical characterization, ultrafast spectroscopy, and first-principles calculations. While all compositions retain an average cubic Pm-3m structure and exhibit a Vegard-like lattice contraction with increasing Br content, strongly nonlinear optical behavior and multiple absorption onsets are observed. First principles calculations reveal that these alloys are more appropriately described by an ensemble of electronically distinct low-energy configurations arising from an underlying polymorphous energy landscape. This configurational diversity redistributes band-edge spectral weight, enables quasi-direct transitions at Γ, and provides a microscopic explanation for the broadband absorption and anomalous bandgap evolution. Transient absorption spectroscopy further supports the presence of different compositiondependent electronic environments and reveals prolonged carrier lifetimes for mixed-halides, consistent with alloy-disorder-induced localization. From an applicative perspective, these materials show remarkable water stability and efficient photothermal energy conversion enabling their use in a proof-of-concept solar water evaporation setup. These findings establish Ag3SI1-xBrx antiperovskites as water-stable, low-toxicity, broadband-absorbing materials and demonstrate the importance of polymorphous local structure in governing their optical response.

item.title: Dual-atom Cu/Ni-Loaded SAPO-34 Facilitates Acetic Acid Production under Non-Thermal Plasma Catalysis
item.description: Directly using CO2 for the efficient C-C coupling with methane into valuable chemicals under atmospheric conditions provides an appealing pathway for the greenhouse gases resourcefulness utilization, but owing to the chemical inertness of methane and the low activity of CO2, this remains a significant challenge. Nonetheless, non-thermal plasma (NTP) offers a distinctive approach for achieving thermodynamically unfavorable reactions at mild conditions by virtue of its non-equilibrium characteristics. Herein, we first report an NTP-assisted catalysis for the efficient CC coupling of methane and CO2 to yield acetic acid over a novel Cu1Ni1@SAPO-34 heteronuclear diatom catalysts under ambient conditions (20 °C, 1 atm), which achievement a remarkable 1204.22 μmol·gcat-1·h-1 productivity and 26.49 % selectivity of acetic acid with acids account for up to 90.02 % of the liquid oxygenates selectivity. Advanced structural microscopic technology revealed that Cu and Ni dual-metal uniformly dispersed on SAPO-34 zeolites in the form of heteronuclear diatoms, which can powerfully promote the reactants dissociation to form some free radicals (e.g. CH3*, CO2*, etc.). Furthermore, in-situ spectroscopic characterizations and theoretical calculations demonstrated the synergistic effect between Cu and Ni diatoms facilitate the occurrence of efficient C-C coupling to generate acetic acid which resulting in significantly en-hancement the selectivity and production of acetic acid.

item.title: Spatial arrangement of bonds governs the thermodynamics of multivalent DNA origami interfaces
item.description: Multivalency, the simultaneous engagement of many weak bonds, underlies recognition between cells, viruses, and proteins and enables assembly of DNA origami into micrometer-scale structures. Predicting the stability of a multivalent interface is difficult because each bond's contribution depends on the number, strength, and arrangement of the other bonds and on the scaffold that presents them, which rarely vary independently. We use DNA origami tiles with 11 addressable sites along one edge to build 236 interfaces in which bond number, strength, and arrangement are set independently, and measure their melting by FRET. Multivalency stabilizes interfaces far beyond any single bond. Once two tiles dock, each further bond finds its partner at an effective concentration about 105-fold above the tile concentration. Stability nevertheless grows subadditively, because only part of an interface melts as one unit and added bonds contribute only insofar as they are formed near the interface melting temperature. Arrangement matters as much as identity: interfaces built from the same bonds lose stability as bonds spread apart, and moving one bond away from two fixed bonds costs 2.5–3 °C per skipped site. A three-parameter multivalent model in which each bond’s effective concentration decays with its distance from the others predicts held-out melting temperatures to within 1.3 °C, outperforming a gradient-boosted regressor. Coarse-grained simulations of polymer-tethered binders reproduce this loss and show that linker and scaffold rigidity set how well binding sites stay in register. These results give design rules and a predictive tool for multicomponent DNA assembly and other multivalent systems.

item.title: Learning from formulation revisions for closed-loop electrolyte optimization
item.description: Electrolyte design for high-energy batteries remains largely empirical, as compositional changes introduce complex trade-offs among ion transport, solvation and interfacial stability. Although data-driven approaches have advanced electrolyte property prediction and candidate optimization, improvements in individual properties do not necessarily translate into better performance in working batteries. Meanwhile, empirical knowledge about how researchers have modified electrolyte formulations to address specific design challenges remains largely untapped. Here we develop a framework that reconstructs literature-reported formulation changes as directed transitions. Within this framework, the Transition-grounded Revision Agent for Closed-loop Electrolyte Optimization (TRACE) learns composition- and objective-dependent modification preferences, grounds molecular proposals, and uses physics-based feedback to guide successive revisions. Starting from a conventional LiPF6-based EMC/PC electrolyte, the framework explores additive and solvent modifications and identifies an FEMC/TFPC (8:2) formulation with increased anion participation in Li+ solvation while maintaining ionic conductivity. In 5-Ah pouch cells, the capacity decay rate decreases from 0.085% to 0.042% per cycle. Under a separate leanelectrolyte configuration, high-energy cell achieves 509 Wh kg-1 and retains 498 Wh kg-1 after 200 cycles. These findings show how historical formulation experience can be transformed into evidence-grounded, feedback-guided decisions for electrolyte design.

item.title: HFC-134a Upcycling via Alkaline Hydrolysis
item.description: As hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) are gradually phased out by global regulations, there is an increasing need for efficient destruction methods to treat the now waste refrigerants and legacy material. Current methods such as incineration and plasma are energy intensive, produce corrosive and/or toxic compounds, and may generate other fluorinated gas emissions. Continuous flow alkaline hydrolysis (AH) is a commercial method for the treatment of perfluoroalkyl substances. This work explores the AH process for the treatment of HFC-134a, an HFC commonly used in large scale refrigeration and vehicle air conditioning. We demonstrate not only >90% destruction and defluorination, but also the conversion of the waste refrigerant to glycolate and fluoride salts, useful compounds for various industries. We also analyze the kinetics and propose a mechanism for the conversion, providing insight into optimization of continuous flow AH in scalable HFC upcycling.

item.title: Initial long-range order biases activation-induced atomic restructuring in Pt–Co nanoparticles
Atroposelective synthesis of biaryls with artificial SNAr enzymes
item.description: Artificial enzymes have been widely employed for the construction of molecules featuring point chirality. However, application of these biocatalysts for the assembly of less common stereogenic elements such as chiral axes, which are a key feature of numerous bioactive compounds and chiral catalysts, is far less explored. Here, we show that SNArases previously developed to set point chirality can also be used to construct axially chiral biaryl motifs. We identifed a pair of miniature enantiocomplementary NTF2-like enzymes (SNArax1 and SNArax2) that differ by only four mutations and allow enantiodivergent synthesis of biaryls through desymmetrizing SNAr processes. These enzymes can process a broad range of dichloropyrimidine electrophiles and (thio)phenol nucleophiles to construct a diverse array of pyrimidine-containing biaryls with excellent yields (up to 99% yield) and enantioselectivities (up to >99% e.e.). The products generated feature a halide substituent that serves as a functional handle for further synthetic manipulations that proceed with retention of stereochemical information. Computational modelling of SNArax1 and SNArax2 shows that their opposing selectivity profiles can be traced to an altered backbone conformation in the C-terminal region that subtly reshapes the electrophile binding pocket. This study expands the synthetic capabilities of artificial SNAr biocatalysts and shows how these systems can be adapted to accurately control chiral axes within complex three-dimensional structures.

item.title: A Small Molecule Mimic of α-ketoglutarate Dependent JmjC Domain Containing Lysine Demethylase Enzyme
item.description: Regulation of epigenetic modifications is a natural process important in the mammalian development as well defense system. Their dysregulation leads to autoimmune disease conditions and cancers. Understanding the cause of their aberrant occurrences can lead to better therapies. The Lysine methylation being a key epigenetic modification, is dynamically and tightly regulated by Lysine methyltransferases and Lysine demethylases. Its demethylation mechanism, however, needs more thorough understanding. Here, we report a small molecule chemical model of the JmjC domain containing Lysine demethylases that mimics the removal of methyl group from methylated Lysine analogues. Our studies agree with the proposed mechanism of demethylation catalysed by the non-heme Fe(II) containing based dioxygenases whereby we have detected the formation of an intermediate ‘Hydroxy-DMA’ as well as formaldehyde as a byproduct of demethylation. We also confirmed the same mechanism of demethylation on the actual substrate, N,N-dimethyl-L-Lysine, via LCMS. This chemical model provides a mechanistic insight into Lysine demethylation and highlights the potential of chemical models in understanding the fundamental chemistry of epigenetic regulation via Lysine demethylation.

item.title: Circularly polarized luminescence in boron- and nitrogen-embedded helicenes: molecular design, performance benchmarks and device applications
item.description: Boron- and nitrogen-embedded helicenes combine helical chirality with a conjugated B,N-containing backbone. Some multiple-resonance emitters also exhibit narrow emission bands and high photoluminescence quantum yields (Φ). Comparing their circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) requires distinguishing solution, film and device measurements and identifying the electronic transitions that give rise to the absorption and emission dissymmetry factors. We examine four aspects of molecular design and device performance: electronic structure, excitedstate dynamics, transition dipole moments and configurational stability. The review covers 29 B,Ncontaining entries and six classes of controls. We record the medium, physical state and source of each measurement and recalculate CPL brightness as BCPL = εΦ|glum|/2 where all three inputs can be traced. Across 20 compounds with Φ and |glum| measured in the same medium, the correlation is weakly negative (Pearson r = −0.331, Spearman ρ = −0.271) and sensitive to the scaffolds represented. Thirteen entries allow comparison of the dissymmetry factors of corresponding absorption and emission bands in the same medium. Molecular and device benchmarks include |glum| = 0.048 for [10]HAB and a red (M,M)-RBNN device combining a maximum external quantum efficiency of 36.6% with gEL = +1.91 × 10 3. Six pairwise - relationships and nine diagnostic questions distinguish structural interpretations supported by comparisons within a series from those that still require emitting-state transition moments, enantiomeric purity after processing or device measurements at operating luminance.

item.title: Benchmarking Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory Plus One Double (TDDFT-1D) for Potential Energy Surfaces
item.description: Time-dependent density functional theory plus one double (TDDFT-1D) improves on conventional TDDFT by including one specially chosen doubly excited electronic configuration. In this study, we evaluate the ability of that method to describe the ground-and excited-state potential energy surfaces (PESs) of selected model compounds relevant to photochemistry. We find that its accuracy is highly dependent on the given test case. For some systems with relatively little multiconfigurational character, the calculated PESs coincide very closely with benchmark data derived from high-level wavefunction-based calculations. In the most favorable cases–methylene and azomethane–and with specific choices of adjustable simulation parameters, TDDFT-1D PESs follow the benchmark data to around 0.2 eV. For some others, the calculated PESs are distorted to a varying degree. In order to pave the way for future studies employing TDDFT-1D, we identify some specific situations where it may potentially fail, and which should be therefore avoided.

item.title: Chemotype-Symmetric Junction-Tree VAE for SARS-CoV-2 Mpro Inhibitor Design
item.description: The main protease (Mpro) of SARS-CoV-2 is inhibited by covalent drugs such as nirmatrelvir, whose activity comes from a reactive warhead that bonds to the enzyme. Designing safer analogs of these inhibitors is hard because standard drug-likeness objectives optimise away the very warhead that makes them work, and because the fused-aromatic scaffolds they are built on are where generative models most often produce invalid structures. This work presents a generative framework that improves predicted safety while preserving both the warhead and target affinity. Built on a junction-tree variational autoencoder, it represents each molecule as a tree of chemical fragments, encodes it into a continuous latent space, and generates analogs by decoding new points near a known inhibitor’s latent code. A chemotype-symmetric fragment vocabulary gives uniform coverage across the diverse Mpro inhibitor chemotype classes, and a graph-attention attachment scorer conditioned on the latent code reassembles their edgefused ring chemistry at decoding time, reconstructing 19 of 20 top-active targets faithfully. Over this latent space the framework runs a constrained six-objective search that trades off drug-likeness, synthetic accessibility, warhead retention, predicted potency, lipophilicity, and warhead reversibility. Predicted potency comes from a deep-ensemble bioactivity surrogate, whose disagreement across the ensemble also sets an anchor-relative uncertainty cap that gates the search away from chemistry it has not seen. The optimiser is NSGA-III, selected after benchmarking a catalogue of multi-objective methods on this pipeline. From all twenty anchors, spanning five Mpro inhibitor chemotype classes, the framework produces a de-duplicated library of 1,013 analogs and retains the source warhead in 85% of the parents that carry one. A perwarhead analysis shows predicted mutagenicity is governed by the warhead class rather than by covalency, the reversible nitrile of the marketed inhibitors being as clean as non-covalent chemistry while the irreversible chloroacetamide and Michael warheads carry the liability. The final Pareto front of 138 analogs is predicted as safe as or safer than each analog’s own source inhibitor on four of eight ADMET endpoints and at parity on mutagenicity, with the warhead retained in 94% of the front and docked binding within AutoDock Vina’s scoring error of the parents, at a modest predicted-potency cost. The strongest single candidate is a dual-warhead analog of nirmatrelvir, predicted safer than the drug on seven of eight endpoints. This safety advantage over the source inhibitors, obtained without erasing the warhead, is the central result, and one that objectives penalising the covalent warhead cannot reach without discarding the mechanism.

item.title: Are fungi and their enzymes effective for biodegradable microplastics in wastewater? Linking particle retention to polymer-carbon conversion
item.description: Biodegradable microplastics (BMPs) can persist through wastewater treatment and be transferred from water to sludge without substantial polymer degradation, posing potential risks to aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. Fungi can colonize biodegradable polyester particles and produce extracellular enzymes capable of depolymerization, but their effectiveness in continuous municipal wastewater treatment remains uncertain. This critical review examines the relationships among particle retention, fungal enzyme activity, polymer hydrolysis, and the fate of released carbon. We distinguish physical capture from depolymerization, assimilation, and mineralization, drawing on evidence from fungal cultures, isolated enzymes, and mixed microbial systems. Three potential treatment configurations are evaluated: recoverable fungal pellets, attached fungal growth, and enzymatic hydrolysis of concentrated BMP fractions. Their feasibility depends on sustained particle–enzyme contact, catalytic activity under non-sterile conditions, and downstream utilization or recovery of hydrolysis products. We propose evaluation criteria incorporating polymer-specific inventories across effluent, sludge, and retained solids; isotope-based carbon tracing; matched experimental controls; and energy and material accounting. This framework identifies the evidence needed to determine whether fungal interventions achieve genuine reductions in residual polymer discharge rather than merely transferring biodegradable microplastics between environmental compartments.
